records.t: A field guide for starting from zero Build the body. Build the habit. Everything a beginner needs to start calisthenics, built around a 5'9", 150 lb starting point, no equipment, and three focused hours a week. You are not underweight — you are under-muscled . Different problem, different fix. Daily calories ~2,800 kcal A lean bulk. Recalculate for your age and sex → Daily protein 150 g 1 gram per pound of bodyweight. The single most important nutrition number. Sessions 3 / week ~60 minutes each, full body, with a rest day between. Non-negotiable structure. Sleep target 7–9 hrs Muscle is built while you sleep, not while you train. Undersleeping halves your results. Year-1 potential +15–25 lb Realistic first-year muscle gain for an untrained male who eats and sleeps properly. The honest summary, in one paragraph. Pick a small number of hard movements. Do them 3 times a week. Every week, add a rep or make them slightly harder. Eat about 300 calories more than you burn, with 150 g of protein. Sleep 8 hours. Write down what you did. Do that for a year and you will not recognize yourself. Everything below is detail on top of those five sentences — the detail matters, but it is detail. You do not need to feel ready. Ready is built through repetition. What calisthenics actually is (and isn't) Calisthenics is strength training where the resistance is your own body. Push-ups, pull-ups, dips, squats, rows, core holds, and eventually skills like handstands and levers. It is not a separate species of exercise from lifting weights — it obeys exactly the same rules of physiology. Muscle grows when you give it a hard mechanical challenge, repeatedly, with enough recovery and enough protein. A barbell and a pull-up bar are two ways to deliver that challenge. What is genuinely different: What it does better Costs almost nothing. You can start today, on the floor, for $0. Builds control, not just force. Everything else — the program, the exercise ladders, the goals — is an application of what's here. If you understand this page, you can fix your own training forever instead of asking the internet. Muscle is expensive tissue. Your body will not build or keep it unless you give it a reason. The reason is mechanical tension : muscle fibers being forced to produce high force, repeatedly, close to their limit. Sensors in the muscle detect that tension, trigger a signaling cascade, and — if there is enough protein and enough rest — the fibers repair thicker than before. Two separate things improve, on two different clocks: Neural adaptation (weeks 1–8) Your nervous system gets better at using the muscle you already have: recruiting more motor units, firing them faster, and switching off the antagonist muscles that were fighting you. This is why your push-up count can double in a month with almost no visible change. Implication: early rep jumps are real strength but not yet size. Don't panic when the mirror lags the logbook by two months. Hypertrophy (weeks 6 onward) Actual growth of muscle fibers — more contractile protein laid down inside each cell. Slower, and completely dependent on eating enough and sleeping enough. A realistic ceiling for a well-fed untrained male is roughly 1–2 lb of muscle per month in year one, halving in year two, and halving again after that. Implication: your first year is the cheapest muscle you will ever buy. Don't waste it eating 1,800 calories. Connective tissue — tendons, ligaments, joint capsules — adapts on a third , much slower clock: months, not weeks. This mismatch is the single biggest injury risk in calisthenics. Your muscles will be ready for one-arm push-up attempts long before your elbows are. That's why the ladders on this site have rep gates before you move up: the gate isn't about your muscles, it's about buying time for your joints.

One sentence: if the demand does not increase, the adaptation does not continue. Your body adapts to exactly the stress you give it and then stops. Doing 3 sets of 10 push-ups every session for a year produces a person who is very good at 3 sets of 10 push-ups and otherwise unchanged. So every session needs a target that beats last time in at least one dimension. In a gym that's trivially "add 5 lb." With bodyweight you have to be more inventive — which is what the next section is about. The practical test. Open your log. Compare this week's session to the same session three weeks ago. If nothing is measurably harder — more reps, harder variation, slower tempo, less rest, more sets — you are maintaining, not building. Fix it this week.

records.h: 3 · The five levers: making a bodyweight exercise harder
records.t: You can't add plates to your body, but you have five independent dials. Turn one at a time . Turning three at once is how you jump from "too easy" to "can't do it" with nothing in between. Lever How it works Example Use when 1. Reps & sets More total work at the same difficulty. 3×8 push-ups → 3×12 push-ups → 4×12 Always your first move. Cheapest, safest, most measurable. 2. Leverage Change the angle or the distance between your hands and your center of mass, so the same bodyweight produces more torque. Incline push-up (hands on counter) → floor push-up → feet on a chair → pseudo-planche Reps have hit the top of your range (~15–20) and adding more is just cardio. 3. Range of motion Longer range = more work per rep, and more stretch under load, which is a strong growth stimulus. Push-up on the floor → push-up with hands on parallettes so your chest drops below your hands You want more stimulus without changing the movement you're practicing. 4. Tempo, pauses, and eccentrics More seconds of tension per rep; pauses kill the elastic bounce; slow lowering (eccentric) is where you are strongest and where most damage-and-repair happens. Normal push-up → 3 seconds down, 1 second pause at the bottom, 1 second up You have no way to change leverage right now (travel, no equipment) or you're building control for a skill. 5. Stability & limbs Take away a limb or a point of contact. Halving your base of support roughly doubles the demand on what's left, plus adds a big stability tax. Squat → split squat → Bulgarian split squat → shrimp squat → pistol squat The bilateral version is easy and you have no load to add. This is the answer for legs without equipment. There is a sixth lever once you own gear: added external load — a weighted backpack, a dip belt, a band. It's the most precise of all, which is why intermediate calisthenics athletes almost all end up using it for the basics while saving leverage work for skills. See Gear, Tier 2 . Rule of thumb for choosing a lever. If you can do more than ~20 clean reps, the exercise is no longer building much strength — change leverage (lever 2) or limbs (lever 5). If you can do fewer than ~5, it's too hard — go back a rung and use reps (lever 1) to build up. The productive band for a beginner is roughly 5–15 clean reps .

records.h: 4 · Sets, reps, and how much total work
records.t: What rep ranges do The old story — "1–5 for strength, 6–12 for size, 15+ for endurance" — is roughly directionally right but far too rigid. The current evidence says that if you take sets close to failure, anything from about 5 to about 30 reps builds a similar amount of muscle . What changes across the range is what else you get, and how unpleasant it is. Reps Primarily builds Notes for calisthenics 1–5 Maximal strength, neural efficiency Where skill work lives (one-arm push-up, muscle-up, lever holds). Hard on joints. Not where a beginner should spend most of their time. 6–12 Size, with good strength carryover Your home range. Best balance of stimulus, joint stress, and time. Most of this program lives here. 13–20 Size, muscular endurance Fine and useful, especially for legs, core, and early push-ups when you have no way to add difficulty. Sets get genuinely miserable near failure. 20+ Endurance; diminishing size returns Usually a signal you've outgrown the variation. Time to change a lever — not to do 50 push-ups. How many sets — the volume question Volume is normally counted in hard sets per muscle group per week (a "hard set" = a working set taken within a few reps of failure; warm-ups don't count). Below ~6 sets/week: maintenance at best. You will not grow much. 10–20 sets/week: the productive zone for nearly everyone. This program lands you around 10–14 per major muscle group, which is right for someone who is new and whose connective tissue is unconditioned. Above ~25 sets/week: returns flatten hard and recovery cost climbs. This is where beginners who read too many forums end up, get exhausted, and blame the program. Start at the low end. You want the smallest dose that still produces progress, because that leaves you room to add volume later when progress stalls. If you start at 25 sets a week, you have nowhere to go but sideways. Counting example. In this program, a push-up appears in Session A (4 sets), Session B (3 sets), and Session C (4 sets), plus dips and pike push-ups also hit the triceps and shoulders. So your chest is getting ~11 direct sets a week and your triceps closer to 16 including the indirect work. That is right in the productive zone. This is also why you don't need to add "arm day" — the arms are already working every session.

records.h: 5 · Proximity to failure — the RIR scale
records.t: RIR = Reps In Reserve : how many more clean reps you could have done when you stopped the set. RIR 2 means you stopped with two left in the tank. RIR 0 is true failure. RIR Feels like When to use it 4–5 Comfortable. Bar speed unchanged. Warm-up sets, deload weeks, technique practice, skill work. 2–3 Reps are slowing, you're working, but form is clean. Your default. Nearly all of your working sets, especially weeks 1–8. Almost all the growth, a fraction of the fatigue. 0–1 The last rep grinds; the next one would break down. Last set of an exercise, occasionally. Isolation and core work where failure is safe. Rep-max testing days. Beyond failure Form collapses, you cheat the rep out. Basically never as a beginner. It buys nothing extra and costs days of recovery. Beginners are systematically bad at judging RIR — studies find untrained lifters typically stop 4–6 reps earlier than they think they did. The fix is to occasionally take one set to true failure so you learn what the edge feels like. Once a week, on your last set of one exercise, go until you genuinely cannot complete a clean rep. Then calibrate everything else against that memory. Never take these to failure: anything overhead where a collapse drops you on your head (handstand push-ups, wall holds), anything where failure means falling from a bar with your body extended (front lever, muscle-up attempts), and skill work generally. Failure is for movements where the worst case is that you slowly sink to the floor.

Tempo is written as four numbers: eccentric / pause at bottom / concentric / pause at top . So a push-up at 3-1-1-0 means 3 seconds lowering, 1 second paused at the bottom, 1 second pressing up, no pause at the top. Eccentric (lowering) is the phase you're strongest in — you can lower about 1.3× what you can lift. That's the whole reason negatives work as a progression: you can train a pull-up before you can do one. Pauses at the bottom kill the elastic rebound and force the muscle to produce force from a dead stop in a stretched position. Brutally effective and completely free. The concentric should be intentional, not slow. Push with the intent to move fast even when the rep is grinding — that's what recruits high-threshold motor units. Default tempo for everything in this program: 2-0-1-0 . Two seconds down, no bounce, controlled up. If you find yourself bouncing, dropping, or using momentum, you are too high on the ladder — drop a rung.

Resting too little is the most common self-sabotage in bodyweight training, because sets feel "light" so people rush. Insufficient rest means your next set is limited by breathlessness rather than by muscular fatigue — which means less mechanical tension, which means less growth. Exercise type Rest Why Hard compound work (pull-ups, dips, push-ups, split squats) 2–3 min Full recovery of the phosphocreatine system; lets you actually load the muscle on set 3. Skill / max-strength practice (handstand, levers, negatives) 2–4 min Skill degrades with fatigue. Practicing tired teaches you the wrong movement. Core, calves, accessory 60–90 sec Smaller muscles, faster recovery, low systemic cost. Conditioning finisher 30–60 sec Here the breathlessness is the point. Superset your rest. A 60-minute session with 3-minute rests sounds impossible until you pair non-competing movements: do a push exercise, rest 90 s, do a pull exercise, rest 90 s, back to push. Each muscle still gets 3+ minutes, but you're never standing around. The program is built this way.

records.h: 8 · Frequency and why three full-body days wins
records.t: After a hard session, muscle protein synthesis stays elevated for roughly 24–48 hours in a trained person, then returns to baseline. If you only train chest once a week, that muscle spends five of seven days not growing. Hitting each muscle 2–3 times per week keeps it elevated more of the time — and the research consistently favors 2+ over 1 when weekly volume is matched. Three full-body days gives you: Every major pattern trained 3×/week — near-optimal frequency. Lots of practice reps of each movement, which matters enormously when the movements are also skills. Missing one day costs 33%, not 100%. With a 5-day bro split, missing leg day means legs get nothing that week. A full rest day between every session, which is exactly what unconditioned tendons need. The classic bodybuilding split (chest day, back day, arm day) works fine for people on their fourth year with 6 days to spend. For you, right now, it is strictly worse.

This is the single mechanism you'll use to advance for the next two years, so learn it properly. Every exercise gets a rep range and a set count . Start at the bottom of the range. Example: push-ups, 3 sets of 6, range 6–12. Each session, try to add reps to any set that isn't at the top of the range. 3×6 → 7/6/6 → 7/7/6 → 7/7/7 → 8/7/7 … When every set hits the top of the range (3×12) with clean form and 1–2 RIR, you have earned the next rung. Move to the harder variation and reset to the bottom of the range (e.g. 3×6 feet-elevated push-ups). It will feel like going backwards. It isn't — you are now producing far more force per rep. Repeat forever. Two properties make this work. First, it is self-regulating : bad sleep or a stressful week just means you add fewer reps, not that the program breaks. Second, it is unambiguous : you never have to guess whether you're ready to progress. The logbook tells you. When you stall. Failing to add a rep for two sessions in a row is noise. Three sessions is a stall. In that order, try: (1) sleep and eat more for a week; (2) add one set; (3) take a deload week ; (4) drop back one rung and rebuild. Do not just grind the same numbers for six weeks hoping it resolves.

Block Time What Why in this order General warm-up 5 min Raise body temperature: jog in place, jumping jacks, arm circles, leg swings. Break a light sweat. Warm muscle is more compliant and produces more force; cold tissue tears. Specific warm-up 5 min Wrist prep, scapular push-ups, scapular pulls, band pull-aparts, deep squat hold, then 1–2 easy sets of your first exercise. Primes the exact joints and patterns you're about to load. Wrists and shoulders especially. Skill practice 8 min Handstand or L-sit work, done fresh , well short of failure. Skills are nervous-system learning. Practice them tired and you learn the tired version. Main strength 30 min Your 2–3 hardest compounds — the pulling and pressing patterns — paired to overlap rest. Hardest work when you're freshest. This block is what drives the adaptation. Accessory & core 10 min Legs, core, and whatever's lagging. Shorter rests. Lower skill demand, so fatigue matters less here. Cooldown 3 min Easy stretching of what you just worked, nasal breathing, log your session. Mostly for the logging habit and to downshift. Stretching does not prevent soreness — but the logging genuinely matters.

Form advice online is 90% noise. Here is the whole thing in five rules: Full range of motion. Chest to the floor. Chin over the bar. Hip crease below the knee. Partial reps are the most common way people fake progress. If you can't do full range, the variation is too hard — regress. Control both directions. If you're falling rather than lowering, you're throwing away the most productive half of every rep. Brace your midsection. Before each rep: exhale slightly, then tighten your abs as if bracing for a punch, and squeeze your glutes. This locks your ribcage to your pelvis. Half of "bad push-up form" is just an unbraced core letting the hips sag. Breathe out on the effort. Inhale on the way down, exhale as you press or pull. Don't hold your breath through multiple reps. Move the joints through paths they like. Elbows around 45° from your torso in a push-up, not flared to 90°. Shoulders pulled down and back before you pull, not shrugged into your ears. Knees tracking over your toes, not collapsing inward. Everything else — hand width, foot position, exactly where you look — is personal and you will find your own version within a few weeks. The way to check your form without a coach: film one set from the side with your phone every couple of weeks. You will immediately see the sagging hips or the half-range reps that felt fine from the inside.

records.h: 12 · The six patterns that must all be trained
records.t: Programs go wrong when they become a list of favorite exercises instead of a balanced set of patterns. Every week you need all six. A good sanity check for any program: can you assign every exercise in it to one of these rows, and is every row occupied? Pattern Trains Your movements Horizontal push Chest, front delts, triceps Push-up family, dips (partly) Horizontal pull Mid-back, rear delts, biceps Inverted rows, table rows, band rows Vertical push Shoulders, triceps, upper chest Pike push-ups → handstand push-ups Vertical pull Lats, biceps, forearms, grip Pull-ups / chin-ups and their regressions Legs — squat & hinge Quads, glutes, hamstrings, calves Squat → split squat → pistol; glute bridge → Nordic curl Core — anti-extension & anti-rotation Abs, obliques, deep stabilizers, hip flexors Dead bug, hollow hold, plank family, leg raises, L-sit Balance push and pull roughly 1:1, and if anything, favor pull. Almost everyone starts with a strong-ish chest and a weak upper back, then does more push work because it's easier and more visible. The result is rounded shoulders, a forward head, and eventually shoulder pain. Extra rows are the cheapest insurance in all of training.

records.h: 13 · Twelve mistakes that will cost you months
records.t: Mistake What it costs Fix Program hopping every 3 weeks Everything. No program can show results before ~8 weeks. Commit to 12 weeks before you judge anything. Not logging workouts You cannot apply progressive overload if you don't know last week's numbers. Use the tracker. Every set, every session. Half-range reps to inflate the count Trains a shorter, weaker range and lies to your logbook. Full range or regress. Film yourself monthly. Eating like you're trying to stay 150 lb The most common reason a skinny beginner sees no change. You literally cannot build tissue from a deficit for long. Eat ~2,800 kcal, 150 g protein. Too much push, not enough pull Shoulder pain in month 4–8, and a physique that looks worse from behind. Match or exceed push volume with pull volume. Skipping legs The classic calisthenics look: big arms on chicken legs. Also worse athleticism and a weaker core. Legs every session. They're in the program for a reason. Chasing advanced skills in month 1 Muscle-up and front lever attempts on unconditioned tendons cause elbow and shoulder tendinopathy that lasts months. Earn the rep gates. They exist to protect connective tissue. Rushing rests to "keep the burn" Turns strength training into cardio. Less tension, less growth. Time your rests. 2–3 min on compounds. Training through sharp or joint-line pain Turns a 2-week annoyance into a 6-month problem. Read the pain rules . Sharp, joint-located, or worsening = stop. Sleeping 5–6 hours Directly and measurably reduces muscle gain, increases fat gain, and blunts strength. 7–9 hours, consistent bedtime. Protocol. Adding 40 minutes of "extra" work because you feel good Recovery debt that shows up two weeks later as a stall. Do the program. Add volume deliberately, not emotionally. Comparing yourself to Instagram Demoralization, then quitting. Those are 5–15 year training ages, often with unusual leverages and sometimes drugs. Compare to your own logbook from 8 weeks ago. That's the only honest comparison.

Term Meaning Rep One complete execution of a movement, start to finish. Set A group of reps done back to back without rest. Hard / working set A set taken within ~3 reps of failure. The kind that counts toward volume. RIR Reps In Reserve — how many you left in the tank. RPE Rate of Perceived Exertion, 1–10. RPE 8 ≈ RIR 2. Two scales for the same thing. Concentric The shortening/lifting phase — pressing up out of a push-up. Eccentric / negative The lengthening/lowering phase. You're ~30% stronger here, which is why negatives are a progression tool. Isometric A hold with no movement — plank, L-sit, handstand, dead hang. Progression / regression A harder / easier version of the same movement pattern. Volume Total work, usually counted as hard sets per muscle per week. Deload A planned easy week to let fatigue dissipate and connective tissue catch up. Scapular retraction / depression Pulling your shoulder blades together / pulling them down away from your ears. The setup position for nearly every pull. Hollow body Ribs down, lower back pressed flat, pelvis tucked. The fundamental calisthenics core position. Straight-arm strength Force produced with elbows locked (planche, lever, L-sit). Loads tendons far more than bent-arm work — earn it slowly. GPP General physical preparedness — baseline conditioning that lets you recover between sets and sessions. DOMS Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness. Peaks 24–48 h after training. Not a measure of a good workout. TDEE Total Daily Energy Expenditure — the calories you burn per day, all in. Exercise library Every movement, arranged as a ladder Calisthenics has no dumbbell rack, so difficulty comes from ordered progressions instead. Each ladder below runs from "you can do this today, at 150 lb, with no equipment" to genuinely advanced. Each rung has a gate : the exact performance that earns you the next rung. How to use this page. You do not do every exercise here. You pick one rung per ladder — whichever one puts you in the 5–15 clean rep range — and that is your exercise until you clear its gate. The program tells you which ladders to use on which day. Come back here when you clear a gate, or when something hurts and you need a regression. Five minutes, every session, before anything else. Wrists and shoulders take the most abuse in calisthenics and get the least attention; this is what keeps them healthy. Wrist prep sequence 2 min · every session Your wrists are about to hold your entire bodyweight in extension — a position they never otherwise experience. Do all of these on the floor, 10 slow reps or a 20-second hold each: Palms down, fingers forward. Rock forward and back over your hands, keeping palms glued down. Palms down, fingers pointing back at your knees. Rock gently backward. This one stretches the forearm flexors hard — go easy. Backs of hands down, fingers pointing back. Rock gently. Stretches the extensors. Fists down, knuckles flat. Rock forward and back. Builds the option to train on fists when wrists are cranky. Fingertip pushes. On all fours, push down through fingertips only, 10 reps. Wrist circles , 10 each direction, with fingers interlaced. Why it matters: wrist pain is the #1 reason beginners abandon handstand work. Two minutes a session prevents almost all of it. Shoulder prep: dislocates, pull-aparts, scapular work 2 min · every session Towel/band dislocates × 10. Hold a towel wide overhead, arms straight, and take it back behind you and return. Go wider if it pinches. Never force it. Band pull-aparts × 15. Arms straight in front holding a light band, pull it apart to chest level, squeezing shoulder blades together. Best single exercise for beginner shoulder health. Scapular push-ups × 10. In a push-up plank with locked elbows , let your chest sink between your shoulder blades, then push the floor away and round your upper back. Only the shoulder blades move. Scapular pulls × 10 (once you have a bar). Hang with straight arms, then pull your shoulder blades down and back to raise your body an inch or two. No elbow bend. This is the missing skill in 90% of failed pull-ups. Arm circles 10 forward, 10 back, big and slow. Lower body prep: leg swings, deep squat hold, ankle rocks 1–2 min Leg swings 10 front-to-back and 10 side-to-side per leg, holding a wall. Deep squat hold, 30–60 s. Sit in the bottom of a squat, heels down, elbows inside knees pushing them out. If your heels lift, put a book under them and work toward flat. Ankle rocks × 10/side. Half-kneeling, drive your knee forward past your toes keeping the heel down. Ankle mobility is the hidden limiter in pistol squats. Glute bridges × 15 to wake up the glutes before squatting.

records.t: Trains: pectorals, front deltoids, triceps, serratus anterior, and (if you brace properly) the entire anterior core. This is your bread and butter for the first year. Wall push-up Hands on a wall at chest height, body in a straight line, step feet back. Gate: 3 × 20 clean, controlled reps . High incline push-up Hands on a kitchen counter or a sturdy desk (~36"). Gate: 3 × 15 . Low incline push-up Hands on a chair seat, couch arm, or stair (~18"). Gate: 3 × 15 . Knee push-up On the floor from the knees, hips fully extended — no piking. Gate: 3 × 15 . Negative push-up Start at the top on your toes, lower for a 5-count to the floor, then reset from the knees. Gate: 3 × 8 with the last rep still taking 5 seconds. Full push-up Chest to the floor, straight line from ears to ankles. Gate: 3 × 12 at 2-0-1-0 tempo. Feet-elevated (decline) push-up Feet on a chair 12–18" up. Shifts load toward the upper chest and shoulders. Gate: 3 × 12 . Diamond push-up Hands together under the sternum, index fingers and thumbs touching. Heavy triceps emphasis. Gate: 3 × 12 . Deficit push-up (parallettes / books) Hands elevated 4–6" so your chest drops below your hands. Huge stretch under load. Gate: 3 × 12 . Archer push-up Wide hands; lower toward one hand while the other arm straightens out to the side. Gate: 3 × 8 per side . Pseudo-planche push-up Hands at waist level, fingers turned out, shoulders leaning far forward past the hands. Brutal on the front delts and the bridge to planche work. Gate: 3 × 8 . One-arm push-up progression Elevated one-arm → feet wide one-arm → feet together. Years away. Listed so you know the ladder doesn't end. Full push-up — setup, execution, and the five things that go wrong core lift Setup Hands slightly wider than shoulder width, directly under or just below your shoulders — not up by your head. Fingers spread, pointing forward or very slightly out. Grip the floor with your fingertips. Feet together or a few inches apart. Together is harder (less base), apart is more stable. Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs until your body is one rigid plank. Tuck your pelvis slightly so your lower back isn't arched. Push the floor away slightly so your upper back is not collapsed between your shoulder blades — this is called protraction and it protects the shoulder. Execution Inhale. Lower under control over ~2 seconds. Keep elbows at about 45° from your torso — from above, your arms and body make an arrow shape, not a T. Touch your chest (sternum, not your face) to the floor. Nose an inch off the ground. Exhale and press up, driving through the whole hand. Push the floor away rather than thinking about lifting yourself. Lock out fully at the top without letting your hips sag or your shoulders shrug. What goes wrong Sagging hips / arched lower back. Unbraced core. Squeeze glutes harder and tuck the pelvis; if you can't hold it, regress a rung. Piked hips. Usually a cheat to shorten the range. Straight line, ears to ankles. Flared elbows at 90°. The classic shoulder-impingement setup. Pull them in to 45°. Head leading. Chin reaching for the floor while the chest stays high. Keep your neck neutral — eyes at a spot ~1 ft in front of your hands. Half reps. Chest must reach the floor. If it can't, go back to inclines. Nobody is impressed by 40 half push-ups. Variations by emphasis Wider hands → more chest, less triceps, more shoulder stress. Narrower / diamond → more triceps and inner chest. Feet elevated → more upper chest and front delts. Hands elevated → more lower chest, easier overall. Hands turned out ~30° → often kinder to cranky wrists and elbows.

records.t: Trains: lower chest, triceps (heavily), front deltoids. Dips are the closest bodyweight equivalent to a heavy press and are worth building toward. They are also the movement most likely to irritate a shoulder, so respect the depth rule below. Bench dip, knees bent Hands behind you on a chair edge, feet flat and close. Gate: 3 × 15 . Bench dip, legs straight Heels on the floor, legs extended. Gate: 3 × 15 . Bench dip, feet elevated Heels on a second chair. Gate: 3 × 12 . Note: this position is hard on the shoulder — don't live here. Get to parallel bars. Parallel-bar support hold Arms locked, shoulders pushed down away from your ears, body vertical, legs still. Gate: 3 × 30 s . Negative dip Jump or step to the top, lower for a 5-count to upper arms parallel to the ground, step off. Gate: 3 × 5 . Full parallel-bar dip Lower until upper arms are parallel to the floor (~90° elbow), press back to lockout. Gate: 3 × 10 . Weighted or ring dip Add a loaded backpack, or move to rings and add the stability demand. Gate for rings: 3 × 8 with rings turned out at the top. The depth rule. Stop when your upper arms reach parallel with the ground. Going deeper feels impressive and puts the shoulder in maximum extension under load — that is where labrum and biceps-tendon problems come from. Also keep a slight forward lean (chest-focused) or stay vertical (triceps-focused), but do not let your shoulders roll forward and up toward your ears at the bottom.

records.h: Vertical push — pike push-up to handstand push-up
records.t: Trains: deltoids (all three heads), triceps, upper traps, and the whole overhead stability system. This is how you build shoulders without a barbell, and it doubles as handstand preparation. Incline pike push-up Hands on a chair, hips piked high, press with the crown of your head moving toward your hands. Gate: 3 × 12 . Floor pike push-up Downward-dog position on the floor, hips as high as you can, elbows tracking forward. Gate: 3 × 12 . Feet-elevated pike push-up Feet on a chair, torso nearly vertical. This is a genuine overhead press. Gate: 3 × 10 . Wall plank / wall walk Feet on the wall, walk your hands in until your body is vertical, chest facing the wall. Gate: 60 s hold . Chest-to-wall handstand hold Fully vertical, ribs down, glutes squeezed, pushing tall through the shoulders. Gate: 60 s total, in sets. Partial wall handstand push-up Back to the wall, lower a few inches and press back up. Gate: 3 × 5 . Full wall handstand push-up Head lightly touches the floor (on a folded towel), press to lockout. Gate: 3 × 8 . Freestanding handstand push-up Requires a solid freestanding handstand first. Long-term goal. Pike push-up — how to actually do it right core lift Setup: From a push-up position, walk your feet toward your hands until your hips are as high as possible and your torso is as close to vertical as your hamstrings allow. Hands slightly wider than shoulders. Bend your knees if tight hamstrings force your back to round — you want a vertical torso , not straight legs. Execution: Lower the top of your head toward the floor between and slightly in front of your hands, so your head and hands form a triangle. Elbows track forward and slightly out — not flared to the sides. Touch lightly. Press straight back up. Most common error: turning it into a decline push-up by letting the hips drop and pressing forward instead of up. If your chest is going toward the floor rather than your head going down between your hands, your hips are too low. Progress cue: the higher your feet and the more vertical your torso, the more of your bodyweight your shoulders carry. That is your leverage dial.

records.t: Trains: latissimus dorsi, biceps, brachialis, forearms and grip, lower traps, rhomboids, and core. If you only did one calisthenics exercise for life, this would be it. It is also the pattern you cannot properly train without a bar — which is why a $30 doorway bar is the highest-ROI purchase on this site. Dead hang Just hang, shoulders relaxed then actively engaged. Builds grip and decompresses the spine. Gate: 60 s total accumulated , and one unbroken 30 s hang. Scapular pull-up Hang with straight arms; pull your shoulder blades down and back to lift yourself 1–2 inches. Elbows stay locked. Gate: 3 × 10 with a visible 2-inch rise. Feet-assisted / band-assisted pull-up Bar low enough to keep toes on the ground and take some weight, or a resistance band looped over the bar under your knee. Gate: 3 × 8 with the lightest band you own. Negative pull-up Jump or step to the top with your chin over the bar, then lower for a 5-count. Gate: 3 × 5 where the last rep still takes 5 full seconds. First full pull-up Dead hang, chin fully over the bar, no kipping. This is a milestone worth celebrating. Gate: 3 sets of 5 . Pull-up for reps Gate: 3 × 10 strict, full range, controlled negative. Weighted / L-sit / archer pull-up Backpack with books or plates, or hold an L-sit shape throughout, or shift weight toward one arm. Gate for weighted: 3 × 6 with 25 lb . One-arm pull-up progressions Assisted one-arm (towel, other hand on wrist) → one-arm negative → full. Multi-year goal. Pull-up — grip, setup, execution, and why yours is stalling core lift Grip choices Pull-up (overhand/pronated), hands just outside shoulder width — most lat, hardest. Chin-up (underhand/supinated), shoulder width — more biceps, noticeably easier. Start here if you can't do a pull-up yet. Most people get a chin-up 2–4 weeks before a pull-up. Neutral (palms facing each other), if your bar has handles — usually the most shoulder- and elbow-friendly of the three. Very wide grip — popular, shortens the range, increases shoulder stress, doesn't build a wider back any faster. Skip it. Execution Hang with straight arms. Grip hard — wrap your thumb around the bar. Set the shoulders first: pull your shoulder blades down and back, away from your ears. This one step fixes more failed pull-ups than anything else. Squeeze glutes, brace abs, cross or point your feet. Body slightly hollow — do not let your legs swing behind you. Pull your elbows down toward your ribs , not your chin up toward the bar. Drive them into your back pockets. Chin clears the bar. Chest toward the bar. Lower over 2–3 seconds all the way back to straight arms. Full extension every rep. Why yours is stalling You start each rep dead-limp. Set the scapula first. Practice scapular pull-ups. Grip fails before the back does. Add dead hangs at the end of every session. Only doing negatives. Negatives build the top half; you also need assisted concentric work to learn to pull from a dead hang. Not doing rows. A weak mid-back caps your pull-up. Every session has rows for a reason. Bodyweight climbing too fast. Pull-ups are the exercise most punished by weight gain. If your pull-up stalls while you're bulking, that's expected — check reps-per-pound, not raw reps.

records.t: Trains: rhomboids, mid and lower traps, rear deltoids, lats, biceps. This is the anti-hunchback pattern and the most-skipped exercise in beginner calisthenics — partly because it's the hardest to improvise. Do not skip it. Doorway / towel row Loop a towel around a solid door handle (door open, standing on the hinge side so it can't swing), lean back with straight arms, pull your chest to your hands. Adjust foot position for difficulty. Gate: 3 × 15 with feet well forward. Table row (bent knees) Lie under a sturdy table, grip the edge, knees bent, feet flat, pull your chest to the underside. Gate: 3 × 12 . Inverted row, legs straight Under a bar or table, heels on the floor, body in one line, chest to the bar. Gate: 3 × 12 . Feet-elevated inverted row Heels on a chair so your body is horizontal or better. Gate: 3 × 12 . Archer row Pull toward one hand while the other arm straightens along the bar. Gate: 3 × 8 per side . Tuck front lever row Hanging in a tuck front lever, row your chest to the bar. Advanced. Gate: 3 × 6 . One-arm row / full front lever row Long-term. The row cue that changes everything. Lead with your elbows and finish by squeezing your shoulder blades together hard, as if pinching a pencil between them, then pause for one second. Rowing with straight-line arm-bend only and no scapular retraction trains biceps and skips the back entirely.

Trains: quadriceps, glutes, adductors, and — once you go single-leg — a huge amount of balance and hip stability. Bodyweight squats stop being a strength exercise for a healthy 150 lb person within a few weeks. The answer is single-leg work, which is why the ladder moves there fast. Box squat / chair squat Sit back to a chair, tap, stand. Gate: 3 × 15 . Full bodyweight squat Hip crease below knee, heels flat, chest up. Gate: 3 × 20 . Split squat Feet staggered ~2–3 ft apart, both feet on the floor, back knee to just above the ground. Gate: 3 × 12 per leg . Bulgarian split squat Rear foot on a chair. The best leg exercise you can do with no equipment, full stop. Gate: 3 × 12 per leg . Assisted / box pistol squat One-leg squat to a chair or box, or holding a doorframe for balance. Gate: 3 × 8 per leg to a low box. Shrimp squat Hold your rear foot behind you and lower until that knee touches the ground. Gate: 3 × 8 per leg . Pistol squat Full one-leg squat, other leg held straight out in front, no support. Gate: 3 × 5 per leg . Weighted pistol / jumping variations Loaded backpack, or explosive single-leg jumps for power. Bulgarian split squat — the highest-value leg exercise you own core lift Setup: Stand about 2–3 feet in front of a chair or couch. Place the top of your rear foot on it (laces down) — or the ball of the foot if the top of the foot is uncomfortable. Front foot flat, pointing forward. Execution: Lower straight down until your rear knee is an inch off the floor and your front thigh is at or below parallel. Keep most of your weight on the front foot — the back leg is a kickstand, not a driver. Press through the whole front foot, especially the heel, back to the top. Do all reps on one leg, then switch. Adjusting emphasis: a longer stance and a slight forward torso lean hits glutes and hamstrings more; a shorter, more upright stance hits quads more. Do both over time. Common problems: Falling over. Normal for the first 2–3 sessions. Hold a wall or doorframe with one hand until your stabilizers catch up. Front knee caving inward. Actively push the knee out over your second toe. Add glute bridges to your warm-up. Rear leg cramping. Stance is too short. Step further forward. Too easy at 12 reps? Elevate the front foot on a book for more range, or wear a loaded backpack.

records.t: Trains: glutes, hamstrings, spinal erectors. Squatting patterns barely touch the hamstrings, and calisthenics athletes are famous for having none. This is the fix, and it also protects your knees and lower back. Glute bridge On your back, heels close to your butt, drive hips up, squeeze glutes hard at the top for 2 s. Gate: 3 × 20 . Single-leg glute bridge One foot planted, other knee pulled to chest. Keep hips level. Gate: 3 × 15 per leg . Shoulder-elevated hip thrust Upper back on a couch, feet on the floor, thrust hips to full extension. Much larger range. Gate: 3 × 15 . Sliding leg curl On your back with heels on towels (hardwood/tile) or furniture sliders; bridge up, then slowly extend your legs out and curl them back in without letting your hips drop. Gate: 3 × 10 . Single-leg Romanian deadlift Hinge at the hip on one leg, other leg extending straight back, back flat, reach toward the floor. Balance and hamstring stretch. Gate: 3 × 12 per leg , slow. Nordic curl negative Kneel with ankles anchored under a couch or held by a partner; lower your torso forward as slowly as possible, catch with your hands, push back up. Extremely hard. Gate: 3 × 5 with a 4-second lower. Full Nordic curl Lower and return under hamstring power alone. Elite. Multi-year. Nordic curls cause the worst soreness of any exercise in this program. Do one set of three the first time. Not three sets of ten. People who ignore this cannot walk down stairs for four days.

Small, easily trained, and completely ignorable until you notice your calves haven't changed in a year. They respond to high reps and a full stretch. Standing calf raise — 3 × 25, full range, 2-second pause at the top. Single-leg calf raise on a stair — heel drops below the step for a deep stretch, rise to full tiptoe. 3 × 15–20 per leg. This is the version that actually works at 150 lb. Seated / bent-knee calf raise — targets the soleus underneath. Put a loaded backpack on your knee while seated. 3 × 20. Tibialis raises — back against a wall, feet out in front, pull your toes up toward your shins. 3 × 20. Prevents shin splints and balances the ankle.

Trains: rectus abdominis, transverse abdominis, obliques, hip flexors. The core's real job in calisthenics is resisting movement — keeping your body a rigid lever. That's why holds beat crunches here. Dead bug On your back, arms up, knees at 90°. Lower one arm and the opposite leg while pressing your lower back flat into the floor . Gate: 3 × 10 per side , slow, with no lower-back gap. Plank On forearms, glutes squeezed, pelvis tucked, ribs down. Gate: 3 × 60 s . Beyond 60 s, add difficulty rather than time. Tuck hollow hold On your back, lower back pressed flat, knees tucked, shoulders and head off the floor. Gate: 3 × 45 s . One-leg / straight-arm hollow hold Extend one leg, or extend arms overhead. Gate: 3 × 45 s . Full hollow hold Arms overhead, legs straight and low, lower back still flat. The single most transferable core position in calisthenics. Gate: 3 × 45 s . Hollow rock Rock on your lower back while holding a rigid hollow shape. Gate: 3 × 20 . Long-lever plank / ab wheel Walk your elbows well out in front of your shoulders, or use a wheel. Gate: 3 × 30 s / 3 × 10 . How to find the hollow position. Lie on your back and press your lower back into the floor so hard that someone couldn't slide a hand underneath. That is the position. Now lift your shoulders and legs while keeping it. The moment your lower back lifts off, you've gone too far — bend your knees more or lower your legs less. Everyone cheats this. Don't.

Lying knee tuck On your back, hands under your hips, pull knees to chest. Gate: 3 × 20 . Lying straight-leg raise Legs straight, lower until just before your back arches, then return. Gate: 3 × 15 . Hanging knee raise From a dead hang, raise knees above hip height with no swinging. Gate: 3 × 15 . Hanging straight-leg raise Legs straight to horizontal or above, controlled down. Gate: 3 × 12 . Toes to bar Feet touch the bar between your hands, strictly, no kip. Gate: 3 × 8 . The L-sit ladder Foot-supported L-sit Hands on the floor or two books, push down and lift your hips with heels still touching. Gate: 3 × 20 s . Tuck L-sit Knees tucked, feet fully off the ground, shoulders pushed down. Gate: 3 × 20 s . One-leg-extended L-sit One leg straight out, one tucked. Alternate. Gate: 3 × 15 s per side . Full L-sit Both legs straight and horizontal, arms locked, shoulders depressed. Gate: 3 × 15 s . V-sit / manna progressions Legs above horizontal. Advanced gymnastics territory. Why the L-sit is worth the trouble: it simultaneously trains the abs, hip flexors, quads, triceps and — crucially — scapular depression , the strength of pushing your shoulders down away from your ears. That is the exact quality that makes handstands, dips, and levers possible. It also needs almost no space, so it's the perfect skill to practice at home. Note that tight hamstrings will limit your L-sit before your core does; if your legs won't straighten, that's a flexibility problem, not a strength one.

records.t: Side plank — 3 × 45 s per side. Progress by lifting the top leg or extending the top arm overhead. Pallof press (needs a band) — anchor a band at chest height to your side, hold it at your sternum, press straight out and resist the rotation. 3 × 12 per side. Best anti-rotation exercise there is. Bird dog — on all fours, extend opposite arm and leg, hold 3 s, keep hips square. 3 × 10 per side. Superman hold — face down, lift chest and legs, squeeze glutes. 3 × 30 s. Balances all the front-side work. Reverse hyperextension on a couch — hips at the edge, torso supported, lift legs to horizontal. 3 × 15. Suitcase carry — walk 40 yards holding a heavy bag in one hand, staying perfectly upright. Underrated, and you can do it with groceries.

Skills are practiced fresh, before your strength work , well short of failure, and often — 3×/week minimum. They are motor learning, not fatigue accumulation. Ten focused minutes beats one exhausting hour. Handstand Wrist prep Every single session. See above . Non-negotiable. Plank → pike hold Build the straight-body shape and shoulder endurance. Gate: 60 s plank, 45 s pike . Wall walk Feet on the wall, walk hands in until your chest nearly touches. Gate: walk in and back out 5 times . Chest-to-wall handstand hold Belly to the wall, fully vertical, ribs tucked, pushing tall. This is the position you actually want — back-to-wall handstands teach a banana-shaped back. Gate: 60 s . Kick-up to wall (back to wall) Learn to kick up with control and find vertical. Gate: 10 consecutive controlled kick-ups that don't slam into the wall. Heel pulls & toe pulls From the chest-to-wall hold, peel one foot then both off the wall and hold balance for a second. Gate: 3-second free hold . Freestanding handstand Balance with fingertip pressure — press through your fingers when falling forward, through the heel of the hand when falling back. Gate: 30 s . Learn to bail on day one. If you're falling forward, turn your body sideways and step down — a cartwheel exit. Practice it deliberately ten times before you ever try a free handstand. The fear of falling is what stops most people from ever getting off the wall, and knowing you have an exit removes it. Front lever Prerequisites before you start: 8 strict pull-ups, 30-second active hang, solid full hollow hold. Straight-arm work loads the elbows and biceps tendon extremely hard — this is the classic overuse injury in calisthenics, and it comes from starting the lever too early. Active/arched hang Hang with shoulder blades pulled down and back, chest up. Gate: 3 × 30 s . Tuck front lever Hanging, pull your body until your back is horizontal with knees tucked to chest, arms straight. Gate: 3 × 20 s . Advanced tuck Open the knees to ~90° so your thighs come away from your chest. Gate: 3 × 15 s . Single-leg front lever One leg extended, one tucked. Gate: 3 × 10 s per side . Straddle front lever Both legs straight and wide. Gate: 3 × 10 s . Full front lever Body fully straight and horizontal. A genuine multi-year goal. Muscle-up Prerequisites, all of them, before you attempt one: 10 strict pull-ups. 10 strict parallel-bar dips. 5 explosive pull-ups where you pull the bar to your lower chest / sternum , not your chin. A false grip you can hold (thumb over the bar, wrist on top) — or the willingness to learn the transition without it. Then drill the transition specifically: jumping muscle-ups from a low bar, negative muscle-ups (start in the support position, lower slowly through the transition), and straight-bar transitions with band assistance. The muscle-up is 20% strength and 80% learning to rotate your elbows and shoulders around the bar at the top of the pull. Attempting it before the prerequisites just produces flailing and shoulder pain.

records.t: You start with nothing but the floor. Here is the honest mapping of what you can and cannot replace, and what it costs you. You need Floor-only substitute How good is it? Pull-up Towel row on a door handle; table row under a sturdy dining table Adequate for 4–6 weeks. It builds real mid-back and biceps strength but cannot replicate the lat stretch and overhead pull. Get a bar. Inverted row Under a solid dining table, grip the edge. Check it holds your weight first, and put something on the far side so it can't tip. Genuinely good. Many people run this for months. Dip Bench dips between two chairs, or on the edge of a couch Fine to start, then limiting. The behind-the-back arm position is not shoulder-friendly at higher difficulty. Overhead press Pike push-up → feet-elevated pike push-up Excellent. Essentially a full replacement. Leg press / squat rack Bulgarian split squat, shrimp squat, pistol progression Excellent for a beginner. Single-leg work is more than enough at 150 lb for a year or more. Hamstring curl Sliding leg curls on towels; Nordic negatives with feet under a couch Very good and criminally underused. Lat pulldown Nothing floor-only replaces this. This is the gap. It is the whole argument for buying a bar in week 1–4. Hanging leg raise Lying leg raise, reverse crunch Good. Loses the grip and lat involvement. Added weight A backpack loaded with books, water bottles (8.3 lb/gal), or bags of rice Surprisingly good. A backpack with 20 lb of books changes push-ups completely and costs nothing. The program 24 weeks, three days a week, starting on your living room floor This is the actual plan. Three full-body sessions a week, about 60 minutes each, with a rest day between every one. Phase 1 needs nothing but the floor. Phase 2 assumes you've added a pull-up bar. Phase 3 is where it starts getting fun. Schedule Mon / Wed / Fri Or Tue/Thu/Sat. Any pattern with a rest day between sessions works. Session length 55–65 min Including warm-up, skill work, and logging. Weekly sets 10–14 / muscle Right in the productive zone, low enough to leave headroom. Deload Every 6 weeks Weeks 6, 12, 18, and 24 are planned easy weeks. records.h: The six rules that make this work
records.t: Pick your rung from the ladders , not from ego. The correct rung is the one where the bottom of the rep range is genuinely hard and the top is currently out of reach. If you can already do the top of the range, move up. If you can't hit the bottom with clean form, move down. Use double progression . Add reps until every set hits the top of the range, then move up a rung and reset to the bottom. That's the whole progression mechanism, forever. Stop 2–3 reps short of failure on everything except the final set of each exercise, where 1 RIR is fine. Weeks 1–2, stop 4 short. You are building tendons, not testing yourself. Rest 2–3 minutes between hard sets. Use the pairings (A1/A2) so you're never idle: do A1, rest 90 s, do A2, rest 90 s, back to A1. Each muscle still gets three full minutes. Log every set, every session. Exercise, rung, reps per set, and how it felt. The tracker does this. Without a log there is no progressive overload, only guessing. Never skip the warm-up, and never skip legs. These are the two things beginners cut when short on time, and they are the two that cost the most.

Goal: build the habit, learn the six patterns, condition your connective tissue, and establish a logbook. You should finish every session in weeks 1–2 feeling like you could have done more. That is intentional. The volume ramps: week 1 do 2 sets of everything, week 2 do 3, weeks 3–4 do the full sets listed. Split squat / Bulgarian split squat 4 × 8–12 /leg 2 min B1. Push-up (your rung) 3 × 6–12 90 s B2. Towel / table row 3 × 8–12 90 s C. Single-leg glute bridge or Nordic negative 3 × 8–15 90 s Core & finish · 10 min Dead bug 3 × 10 /side 45 s Superman hold 2 × 30 s 45 s Single-leg calf raise 2 × 15 /leg 45 s Week 1 specifically. Do two sets of everything, stop four reps short of failure on every set, and go home. You will be sore anyway — first-time soreness peaks 24–48 hours later and is worst after session 1. It fades permanently after about two weeks. If you go all-out in week 1 you will be too sore to train in week 1, which sets you back further than the "easy" session ever could.

records.t: Goal: your first pull-up, your first full-range push-ups for real sets, and a chest-to-wall handstand hold. This is where the physique change starts to become visible. The structure is the same; the vertical pull replaces some rowing volume, dips move to a bar if you have one, and skill work gets more specific. Foundation / Session A Session A — Push emphasis Exercise Sets × reps Warm-up + wrist/shoulder prep 8 min Skill: chest-to-wall handstand hold 5 × 20–40 s A1. Push-up rung 4 × 6–12 A2. Pull-up rung (negatives / band / full) 4 × 3–8 B1. Pike push-up rung 3 × 6–10 B2. Inverted row 3 × 8–12 C. Bulgarian split squat 3 × 8–12 /leg Hollow hold rung 3 × 30–45 s Dead hang (grip work) 2 × max Foundation / Session B Session B — Pull emphasis Exercise Sets × reps Warm-up + band pull-aparts 8 min Skill: L-sit progression 5 × 15–20 s A1. Chin-up rung (underhand — easier, builds the pull-up) 4 × 3–8 A2. Dip rung 4 × 5–12 B1. Feet-elevated inverted row 3 × 8–12 B2. Push-up (one rung easier) 3 × 8–12 C. Sliding leg curl / Nordic negative 3 × 6–12 Hanging knee raise 3 × 10–15 Side plank 2 × 45 s /side Foundation / Session C Session C — Legs & skill Exercise Sets × reps Warm-up + lower body prep 8 min Skill: wall walk, kick-up practice, heel pulls 10 min A. Pistol progression (box / assisted / shrimp) 4 × 6–10 /leg B1. Pull-up or chin-up rung 3 × 3–8 B2. Pike push-up rung 3 × 6–10 C1. Shoulder-elevated hip thrust 3 × 12–15 C2. Archer or feet-elevated row 3 × 8–12 Single-leg calf raise 3 × 15–20 /leg Hollow rock 3 × 15–20 Getting your first pull-up faster. Do all three of these in the same week, not just one: negatives (build the top position), band- or foot-assisted full reps (learn to pull from a dead hang), and scapular pull-ups plus rows (build the mid-back that initiates the pull). Add one extra "grease the groove" set: every time you walk past your bar on a non-training day, do one easy assisted rep or a 15-second hang. Never to failure, never sore. This single habit gets most people their first rep weeks earlier.

records.t: Goal: pull-ups and dips for real sets, wall handstand push-ups, pistol squats, and your first L-sit. Same three-day structure, but three things change: Sets go up to 4–5 on the two main lifts of each session. Total weekly sets per muscle move toward 14–18. Add external load where a rung is stalling. A backpack with 15–25 lb of books turns a stalled push-up or dip into a productive one and is far better than chasing an exotic variation. See Gear Tier 2 . Skill blocks get longer and more specific — 12 minutes, with an explicit target (30-second free handstand, 15-second L-sit, 20-second tuck front lever). records.h: How to actually run a session
records.t: Before you start: open your log from last time. Write down the exact numbers you're trying to beat today. Do not train without a target — "see how it goes" is how weeks disappear. Warm up properly. 5 minutes general, 3 minutes specific. Then do one easy set of your first exercise at about half the reps. Skill work while fresh. Short sets, long rests, never near failure. If your handstand holds are getting worse rather than better within the block, the block is over — move on. Main lifts in pairs. A1, rest 90 s, A2, rest 90 s, A1… Set a timer; don't eyeball it. Write each set down as you finish it. Not at the end from memory. Note anything unusual: bad sleep, a tweaky elbow, a rep that felt great. Finish with core and accessories at shorter rests, then two minutes of easy stretching for whatever you just worked. Eat within a couple of hours with 30–40 g of protein. The old 30-minute "anabolic window" is a myth, but total daily protein absolutely is not.

A deload is a planned easy week. Fatigue from training accumulates faster than you notice; a deload lets it dissipate so the next block starts fresh, and it gives tendons and joints — which adapt far more slowly than muscle — a chance to catch up. How to deload: keep the same exercises and the same rungs, but cut sets roughly in half and stop 4–5 reps short of failure on everything. Keep skill practice (it's low fatigue and high value). Do not take the week completely off — total rest loses more than it gains, and it breaks the habit. Signal Meaning Reps declining for 2+ sessions across multiple exercises Accumulated fatigue. Deload now, don't wait for week 6. Joints ache before you even start warming up Connective tissue hasn't caught up. Deload and reassess your rungs. Resting heart rate up 5+ bpm for several days Systemic fatigue or you're getting sick. Dreading sessions you used to look forward to Real and predictive. Deload. Sleep getting worse despite being tired Classic overreaching sign.

You are trying to gain weight, so you don't want to burn enormous amounts of energy. But some cardio is genuinely valuable: it improves recovery between sets and sessions, it's strongly protective for long-term health, and at these doses it will not interfere with muscle gain. Type Dose When Why Zone 2 (easy) — brisk walk, easy bike, easy jog where you can hold a conversation 2–3 × 25–40 min/week Rest days or after training Builds the aerobic base that determines how fast you recover between sets. Very low interference with strength. Daily walking 7,000–10,000 steps Throughout the day Health, appetite regulation, and it keeps a lean bulk lean. Costs nothing in recovery. Intervals / sprints Optional, 1 × 10–15 min/week max Not the day before or after leg-heavy sessions Good conditioning, but expensive in recovery and it competes directly with leg training. Optional for a beginner. Long runs (5+ miles) Not while bulking — High interference with strength and a big calorie sink. Revisit later if you want to run.

Situation What to do Missed one session Nothing. Do it the next day, or skip it and continue. Do not double up. Missed a whole week Resume at the same rungs but cut one set for the first week back. You lose almost nothing in a week. Missed 2–4 weeks Repeat the last week you completed at 2–3 sets and 4 RIR, then resume. Expect soreness. Strength returns much faster than it was built. Only have 20 minutes Do the minimum effective session : 3 sets of your push rung, 3 sets of your pull rung, 3 sets of Bulgarian split squats, all supersetted with 60 s rest. That is 80% of the benefit in a third of the time. Sick — symptoms above the neck (runny nose, sore throat) Train at reduced intensity if you feel up to it. Cut sets in half. Sick — symptoms below the neck (fever, chest, body aches, GI) Do not train. Rest until you're a full day symptom-free, then resume at deload volume. Still very sore from last session Train anyway but reduce sets — light movement usually reduces soreness. If it's severe enough to change your form, swap in a different pattern for that day. Traveling with no space or gear Push-ups, split squats, hollow holds, table rows, and a doorway towel row cover every pattern in a hotel room. Keep the habit even at reduced quality. Terrible sleep last night Train, but drop to 3 RIR and skip the last set of each exercise. Don't try to set records on 5 hours of sleep.

By week 24 you should be doing sets of strict pull-ups and dips, holding a wall handstand, and squatting on one leg. At that point you are no longer a beginner and the linear "add a rep every week" approach starts to sputter. Three sensible directions: Weighted basics. Keep the same three-day structure and just add weight to pull-ups, dips, and push-ups. Boring, and by far the most reliable way to keep getting bigger and stronger. Skill specialization. Pick one goal — freestanding handstand, muscle-up, front lever — and give it a dedicated block with the basics on maintenance volume (about half your current sets). Add a fourth day. An upper/lower or push/pull/legs/skill split, if 3 days is no longer enough stimulus and your recovery is genuinely good. What you should not do is switch to a completely different program because progress slowed. Slowing down after six months is not a sign the program failed. It's a sign it worked, and you're now a more advanced trainee for whom progress is simply slower. That is permanent, and it happens to everyone. Previous ← Exercise library Next Goals & metrics →

Goals & metrics How to prove to yourself that it's working Progress in the first year is real but slow enough to be invisible day to day. The only defense against quitting is measurement — numbers that you can compare against your past self. This page tells you exactly what to record, how often, and what "good" looks like at every stage. records.h: The baseline test — do this on day one
records.t: Twenty minutes, once, before you train. These numbers are irreplaceable: in six months you will badly want to know where you started, and there is no way to go back and get them. Repeat the identical test at weeks 9, 12, and 24, and then every 12 weeks forever. Protocol Warm up for 5 minutes — light cardio plus wrist and shoulder prep. Don't test cold. Rest 3 full minutes between every test. This is a strength test, not a circuit. One attempt per test. Every rep must be full range with clean form — a half rep is not a rep . Stop the set the moment form breaks, not when you physically cannot move. Test in this exact order every time. Order affects results, so it has to be constant. If you can't do a movement at all, write 0 . Zero is a real, useful data point — it's the one that will look most dramatic later. # Test Standard Record 1 Max push-ups Chest to the floor, body straight, no rest at the top. Stop when you break form. Reps 2 Max pull-ups (overhand) Dead hang start, chin fully over the bar, no kipping. No bar? Write "n/a" and test max inverted rows instead. Reps 3 Max inverted / table rows Body straight, chest touches the bar or table edge. Note your foot position so you can replicate it. Reps + setup 4 Max dips (bench or bars) Upper arms to parallel. Note which version. Reps 5 Max pike push-ups Head touches the floor between your hands. Reps 6 Max bodyweight squats Hip crease below the knee, heels down. Cap at 50 — beyond that it's a cardio test. Reps 7 Max split squats, left and right Rear knee to an inch off the floor. Record each leg separately — asymmetry is worth knowing about. Reps L / R 8 Plank hold Forearms, hips level, stop when they sag. Cap at 3 minutes. Seconds 9 Hollow hold Your best rung with the lower back flat. Note which rung. Seconds + rung 10 Dead hang From a bar, until your grip gives out. Seconds 11 Wall handstand hold (chest to wall) If you can get up at all. Otherwise record your best wall-walk position. Seconds 12 Deep squat sit Heels flat, how long can you sit at the bottom of a squat comfortably? A mobility, not strength, marker. Seconds Log it in the tracker. The tracker page has a baseline-test form that stores all twelve numbers with a date, so retests sit next to the original and you can see the deltas at a glance.

records.h: What to measure, and how often
records.t: Metric Frequency How Why it matters Every set you do Every session Exercise, rung, reps per set, RIR The only way progressive overload happens. Non-negotiable. Bodyweight Daily, ideally Wake up, use the bathroom, weigh nude, before eating or drinking. Track the 7-day average , never a single day. Daily weight swings 2–4 lb from water, salt, and food volume. Only the weekly average is signal. Tape measurements Every 4 weeks Same time of day, same conditions, relaxed not flexed. See below . Catches muscle gain that the scale hides and shows you where it's landing. Progress photos Every 4 weeks Same spot, same light, same clothing, same poses. See below . The single most convincing evidence, because you can't see gradual change in a daily mirror. Baseline retest Weeks 9, 12, 24, then quarterly The exact protocol above. Objective proof of strength gain that isn't confounded by which rung you happen to be on. Sleep hours Daily Rough estimate is fine — bed time and wake time. When progress stalls, this is usually the culprit, and you'll only spot it if you tracked it. Calories & protein Daily for the first 4 weeks, then spot-check A food app; weigh food for the first two weeks to learn portions. Almost everyone is wrong about how much they eat until they measure it once. Resting heart rate Daily if you have a watch On waking, before getting up. A sustained 5+ bpm rise is an early fatigue or illness warning. Do not measure daily what changes monthly. Weighing daily is fine because you average it. Taking photos or tape measurements weekly is actively harmful — the change is smaller than the measurement noise, so all you see is randomness, and it reads as failure. Four-week intervals, minimum.

You look at yourself every day, so you are the person least able to notice your own change. Photos four weeks apart are shockingly effective, but only if the conditions are constant. Otherwise you're comparing lighting, not muscle. Same time of day — first thing in the morning, fasted, after the bathroom. Food and water visibly change your midsection. Same place, same light. Overhead room lighting, not a window — daylight changes with the season and time. Same clothing — shorts or underwear, no shirt. Same clothes every time. Same phone position — mark a spot on the floor with tape, prop the phone at the same height, use a 10-second timer. Four shots: front relaxed, side relaxed, back relaxed, and front flexed. The relaxed ones are the honest ones; the flexed one is the fun one. Stand normally. Don't suck in on day one and pose hard on day ninety, or you'll fool yourself in both directions. Never delete the early ones, even if you hate them. Especially if you hate them.

Use a flexible cloth or plastic tape. Snug enough not to sag, loose enough not to compress the skin. Measure relaxed for the record (you can also record a flexed arm for fun, but keep the two separate). Take each measurement twice and average. This is the number you want going up. The waist-to-weight rule. While bulking, weight going up is good and waist going up much is not. A useful ratio: for every 4 lb of bodyweight gained, your waist should grow no more than about 0.5 in . If your waist is outpacing that, you're gaining too fast — cut 200 calories a day and reassess in three weeks.

Beginners obsess over lagging indicators — the mirror, the scale — and get discouraged because those move slowest. Watch the leading indicators instead; they respond within days, and they are what cause the lagging ones. Leading — check weekly Sessions completed this week (target: 3) Total reps beaten vs. last week Protein hit on how many days (target: 6/7) Calories hit on how many days Nights with 7+ hours of sleep (target: 6/7) Whether you actually logged every set Lagging — check monthly or quarterly Bodyweight 7-day average trend Tape measurements Progress photos Baseline retest results Milestones ticked How you look in the mirror If all six leading indicators are green for eight weeks, the lagging ones will follow. That is close to a physical law. If they're green and nothing is happening, the diagnostic below applies.

Work down this list in order. The answer is almost always in the first three rows. Check The test The fix 1. Has it been long enough? Fewer than 8 weeks of consistent training. Nothing is wrong. Keep going. Visible change starts around week 8–12. 2. Are you actually eating enough? Is your 7-day average weight higher than it was a month ago? If not, you are not in a surplus regardless of what you think you ate. Add 250 kcal/day and recheck in two weeks. Repeat until the scale moves. 3. Are the numbers going up in your log? Compare this week's sets to four weeks ago. If not, you're not progressively overloading. Check your rungs — you may be stuck on one too hard to add reps to. Regress a rung and rebuild. 4. Are you sleeping? Average under 7 hours. Fix this before changing anything about training. It is upstream of everything. 5. Is protein really at 150 g? Track carefully for three days. Most people who think they hit 150 g are at 90–110. Add a shake and one more protein-dense meal. 6. Are you training hard enough? Take one set to genuine failure. Were you actually 5+ reps away on your normal sets? Recalibrate. Working sets belong at 1–3 RIR. 7. Are you doing too much? More than ~20 hard sets per muscle per week, or adding extra work on rest days. Cut back to the program as written for four weeks. 8. Is the mirror lying? Compare month-1 and month-3 photos side by side, not from memory. This is the most common outcome: real change that you couldn't see because you see yourself every day. Nutrition You cannot build a body out of nothing At 5'9" and 150 lb, undereating is the single most likely thing to stop you. Training is the signal that says "build muscle"; food is the raw material. Get both wrong and nothing happens. Get training right and food wrong, and still almost nothing happens. This uses the Mifflin–St Jeor equation, the most accurate of the common formulas. It is still an estimate — real metabolisms vary by 10–15% either way. The number it gives you is a starting point; the scale over the following three weeks tells you the truth. records.h: Rate of gain — why slow wins
records.t: You can gain weight as fast as you like. You cannot gain muscle as fast as you like — muscle synthesis has a ceiling of roughly 1–2 lb per month for a well-trained, well-fed beginner. Every pound above that rate is fat. Rate Surplus Roughly what you get Verdict +0.25 lb/wk ~150 kcal Nearly all muscle, very little fat Excellent if you're patient. Slow enough that a bad tracking week erases it. +0.4 lb/wk ~300 kcal ~70% muscle, ~30% fat The recommendation. Best ratio of results to fat gain for a beginner. +0.75 lb/wk ~550 kcal ~50% muscle, ~50% fat Acceptable for a few months if you're very lean and impatient. +1.5 lb/wk ~1,000 kcal ~25% muscle, ~75% fat A "dirty bulk." You end up 25 lb heavier, mostly fat, with worse pull-ups and a cut ahead of you. Bodyweight matters more in calisthenics than in any other strength sport, because you are the load. Ten pounds of fat makes every pull-up, dip, handstand, and lever measurably harder — permanently, until you lose it. Ten pounds of muscle makes them easier. That's the whole argument for the slow lane. How to steer. Every Sunday, average your seven morning weigh-ins. Compare to last Sunday's average. Gaining more than 0.5 lb/week? Cut 200 calories a day. Not gaining after three weeks? Add 250 calories a day. Adjust on three-week trends, never on a single day — daily weight swings 2–4 lb from water and food volume alone.

records.h: Protein — the number that matters most
records.t: Protein supplies the amino acids your body assembles into new muscle. It is also the most satiating and the most metabolically expensive macronutrient. If you get exactly one thing right in your diet, get this one. Situation Target For you at 150 lb Building muscle in a surplus 0.7–1.0 g per lb 105–150 g/day Cutting (deficit) 1.0–1.2 g per lb 150–180 g/day Absolute minimum to not lose ground 0.5 g per lb 75 g/day Point of clearly diminishing returns >1.2 g per lb >180 g/day — no added benefit Use 150 g as your daily target. That's 1 g per pound — comfortably above where the research shows benefits plateau, chosen because it's easy to remember and gives you margin for the days you undershoot. Distribution matters more than timing Muscle protein synthesis is stimulated by a dose of protein, and the response peaks around 0.25 g/lb (roughly 30–40 g for you) per meal. Beyond that, extra protein in one sitting mostly gets oxidized rather than doing more building. So: Split across 4 meals of ~37 g each rather than 2 meals of 75 g. Each meal should have an obvious protein source. If you look at a plate and can't point at the protein, it isn't there. Include one before bed — 30–40 g of casein-rich protein (cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, milk, or a casein shake) supports overnight repair through a 7–9 hour fast. The 30-minute post-workout "anabolic window" is a myth. The elevated response lasts many hours. Eat within a couple of hours and you've captured essentially all of it. Plant-based? Aim about 20% higher (roughly 1.2 g/lb) because plant proteins are generally lower in leucine and less digestible, and combine sources across the day — legumes plus grains, soy, seitan, plus a pea/rice protein blend. Soy and pea protein isolate are the two plant proteins that hold up best in muscle-building research.
records.k: Distribution matters more than timing

records.t: Carbs are stored in muscle as glycogen, which is the primary fuel for the kind of hard, repeated sets you're doing. Low-carb training feels flat, reduces the reps you can grind out, and makes recovery worse. They are also, for most people, the easiest way to actually hit a calorie surplus. Target: 3–5 g per lb of bodyweight when bulking — 340–450 g at 150 lb. The calculator lands you around 375 g. Base most of it on minimally processed sources: rice, oats, potatoes, pasta, bread, fruit, beans. These come with fiber and micronutrients. Fast-digesting carbs around training (fruit, white rice, a bagel) are useful but not essential. Total daily intake matters far more. Carbs are not fattening. A calorie surplus is fattening. Carbs are simply the most common source of one.

records.h: Fat — the one you shouldn't cut too low
records.t: Dietary fat is required for hormone production (including testosterone), absorption of vitamins A, D, E and K, and cell membrane structure. Very low-fat diets measurably lower testosterone, which is exactly backwards for someone trying to build muscle. Target: 20–30% of calories , and never below 0.3 g per lb (45 g at 150 lb). The calculator gives you ~78 g. Prioritize: olive oil, avocado, nuts, seeds, fatty fish (salmon, sardines, mackerel), whole eggs. Get omega-3s. Two servings of fatty fish per week, or a supplement. Anti-inflammatory, good for joints and recovery, and most people eat far too little. Fat is calorie-dense (9 kcal/g vs 4 for protein and carbs), which makes it your best tool if you struggle to eat enough — see below .

Not glamorous, but deficiencies here quietly wreck recovery, sleep, and energy. Fiber: 25–35 g/day. Digestion, satiety, cholesterol, blood sugar. From beans, oats, fruit, vegetables, and whole grains. Vegetables and fruit: aim for 5+ servings a day , and vary the colors — different pigments mean different micronutrients. Vitamin D — most people in the US are low, especially in winter or with darker skin. Low vitamin D is linked to reduced strength and worse recovery. 1,000–2,000 IU/day is a cheap insurance policy. Calcium (1,000 mg) and magnesium (400 mg) — muscle contraction, bone density, sleep quality. Dairy, leafy greens, nuts, seeds. Iron and zinc — energy and immune function. Red meat, beans, shellfish. Vegetarians should pay attention here. Sodium. Do not fear salt if you train and sweat. It matters for performance and blood volume. Just get most of it from food you cooked rather than from ultra-processed products.
