records.h: When you genuinely can't eat that much
records.t: If you have been 150 lb your whole life, 2,800 calories will feel like a lot at first. This is normal and it is a solvable engineering problem: reduce the volume of food, not the calories. Drink calories. Whole milk, juice, and smoothies bypass fullness almost entirely. A shake of 8 oz milk + 1 cup oats + 2 tbsp peanut butter + 1 banana + 1 scoop whey ≈ 800 calories and 45 g protein in three minutes. Add fat invisibly. A tablespoon of olive oil on rice, an extra spoon of peanut butter, cheese on everything. 100–150 calories at a time with no added bulk. Choose the less filling version. White rice over brown, juice over whole fruit, dried fruit over fresh. Fiber is important, but you don't need it from every single source. Eat more often, not more per sitting. Five meals of 560 calories is far easier than three of 930. Don't fill up on vegetables at the start of a meal while bulking. Eat the calorie-dense food first, vegetables after. Ramp up. Add 200 calories a week rather than jumping from 2,000 to 2,800 overnight. Appetite genuinely adapts within a few weeks — hunger hormones adjust. Cut back on cardio if you're doing a lot. Every mile run is ~100 calories you now have to eat back.

records.h: How to track without going crazy
records.t: You don't need to weigh food forever. You need to do it accurately for a few weeks so that your eyeball estimates become good, then spot-check. Weeks 1–2: log everything in a food app (MyFitnessPal, Cronometer, MacroFactor, or a spreadsheet). Use a $12 kitchen scale. Weigh everything. This is tedious and it's a one-time education. Weeks 3–4: keep logging but estimate the small stuff. You'll now know that "a chicken breast" is 6 oz and a "handful of nuts" is 1 oz. After week 4: track protein and total calories only, and only on weekdays. Or build 4–5 standard meals you know the numbers for and rotate them. Forever: if the scale stops moving in the direction you want for three weeks, go back to strict tracking for one week to find out what drifted. It's almost always portion creep. Two common tracking errors. First, forgetting to log cooking oil, sauces, and drinks — that's routinely 300–500 hidden calories a day. Second, logging weekdays but not weekends: two big social days can erase an entire week's deficit or surplus. Log the weekend too, at least at first.

Baseline: about half your bodyweight in ounces — 75 oz (a bit over 2 quarts) at 150 lb. Add 16–24 oz per hour of training. Check your urine. Pale straw is right. Clear means you're overdoing it; dark yellow means catch up. Even 2% dehydration measurably reduces strength and endurance and makes training feel much harder than it should. Coffee and tea count toward your total; the diuretic effect is far smaller than the water they contain. Sports drinks are unnecessary for 60-minute sessions. Water and normal salty food cover it.

records.h: Meal timing and eating around workouts
records.t: Total daily intake accounts for the vast majority of the result. Timing is a small refinement, worth getting roughly right and not worth stressing about. Pre-workout (1–3 hours before): a normal meal with carbs and protein. If you train early and can't stomach a meal, a banana and a scoop of whey 30 minutes out is plenty. Don't train stuffed. A large meal within 30–60 minutes of training makes inverted rows, leg raises, and anything upside-down genuinely unpleasant. Post-workout: eat within a couple of hours. Protein plus carbs. The urgency is far lower than the supplement industry implies. Before bed: 30–40 g of slow protein. Cottage cheese, Greek yogurt, milk, or casein. Training fasted is fine if you prefer it and it doesn't tank your performance — but there's no advantage to it when the goal is building muscle, and there is a modest downside in training quality.

Supplement Verdict Dose Notes Creatine monohydrate Worth it 5 g/day, any time, every day The most researched sports supplement in existence, and one of very few that reliably works. Expect a few extra reps per set and a couple of pounds of water inside the muscle. No loading phase needed. Buy plain monohydrate — the fancy forms are marketing. Whey / plant protein powder Useful 1–2 scoops as needed Food in powder form. It does nothing special; it just makes hitting 150 g easy. Skip it if you already hit your protein from food. Vitamin D3 Probably 1,000–2,000 IU/day Widespread deficiency, cheap, and low D is associated with worse strength and recovery. Get tested if you can. Caffeine Works 100–200 mg, 30–60 min pre Genuinely improves training performance and perceived effort. Don't take it within 8 hours of bed — the sleep cost will outweigh the benefit. Omega-3 (fish oil) If you don't eat fish 1–2 g EPA+DHA/day Joint and general health rather than direct muscle gain. Multivitamin Cheap insurance 1/day Not a substitute for vegetables. Useful if your diet is narrow. BCAAs / EAAs Skip — Pointless if you eat adequate protein. You already have all the amino acids. Testosterone boosters Skip — Do not work in anyone with normal testosterone. Pure marketing. Mass gainers Skip — Expensive sugar and cheap protein. Blend your own with oats, milk, and peanut butter for a third of the price. Fat burners Skip — Caffeine plus fillers, at 20× the price of caffeine. Glutamine, HMB, tribulus, ZMA Skip — No meaningful effect in healthy, well-fed trainees. The honest ranking. Sleep > total calories > total protein > training consistency >>> creatine >> everything else. If you spend money on supplements before you have the first four handled, you are buying a rounding error.

Not a moral question — a mechanical one. Alcohol suppresses muscle protein synthesis for roughly 24 hours after a meaningful dose, badly disrupts deep sleep even when you fall asleep faster, contributes 7 empty calories per gram, and reduces the quality of the next day's training. A drink or two occasionally will not undo your progress. Regular heavy drinking will substantially slow it, mostly through the sleep pathway. If you drink, keep it away from training days and don't make it a habit on the night before a session.

At 5'9" and 150 lb with a BMI of 22 and little muscle, this is an easy call: bulk. You are lean enough that you have plenty of room, and cutting from here would leave you skinny rather than defined — "skinny fat" is fixed by building muscle, never by losing more weight. If you are… Do this Why Under ~12% body fat (male) / ~22% (female) Lean bulk Maximum room to build before fat becomes a problem. 12–18% (male) / 22–28% (female) Lean bulk, or recomp at maintenance Both work. As a total beginner you can gain muscle and lose fat simultaneously at maintenance — a window that closes after the first year or so. Above ~20% (male) / ~30% (female) Cut first, for 8–16 weeks Nutrient partitioning is better when leaner, and lower bodyweight makes every calisthenics movement easier. When to stop bulking: when your waist has grown more than about 2 inches, when you've reached roughly 18% body fat, or when pull-ups have clearly gotten harder from the added weight. Then run an 8–12 week cut at a 20% deficit with protein at 1.2 g/lb, keep training the same, and come back leaner and bigger than you started.

records.h: Nutrition mistakes that cost the most
records.t: Mistake Why it hurts Thinking you eat a lot when you don't The universal skinny-beginner error. If your weight isn't going up, you are not in a surplus — no matter how full you feel. The scale doesn't negotiate. Chasing "clean" eating instead of enough eating Chicken, broccoli, and rice is very filling and very hard to eat 2,800 calories of. Food quality matters; food quantity matters more when the goal is growth. Dirty bulking Gaining 1.5 lb a week gets you fat, makes pull-ups worse, and buys a long cut later. Skipping breakfast then trying to catch up Hard to eat 2,800 calories in two meals. Poor protein distribution too. Drinking calories you didn't count Soda, juice, and coffee drinks are easily 400–600 calories a day, invisibly. Chronically low fat Wrecks hormones, absorption, and mood. Never below 0.3 g/lb. Cutting carbs while trying to build Flat training, worse recovery, fewer reps. Carbs are the fuel for exactly the work you're doing. Changing calories every week You can't read a trend through the noise. Give any change three weeks. Buying supplements before fixing food You cannot supplement your way out of eating 1,900 calories a day. Weighing yourself once and panicking Daily weight swings 2–4 lb from water, salt, and gut contents. Only the 7-day average is real. Previous ← Goals & metrics Next Recovery & injury →

Recovery & injury Training is the stimulus. Recovery is where you actually grow. Nothing improves during a workout — you leave a session temporarily weaker than you arrived. The adaptation happens in the 24 to 72 hours afterward, and only if you sleep, eat, and give the tissue a chance. This page is about not sabotaging the part that does the work. On this page Sleep — the protocol Rest days & active recovery Soreness vs. injury The pain traffic light Tendons and why they lag The five common calisthenics injuries Daily mobility routine Stretching — when and which kind Fatigue management & deloads Signs you're doing too much Stress, and why it counts as training load

Sleep is the most powerful recovery tool available and it is free. Restricting sleep to 5–6 hours a night measurably reduces muscle protein synthesis, lowers testosterone, raises cortisol, increases the proportion of weight gained as fat rather than muscle, degrades reaction time and coordination (which matters for handstands), and roughly doubles injury risk in athletes. No supplement, program, or diet compensates for it. Target 7–9 hrs Actual sleep, not time in bed. Budget ~30 min extra for falling asleep. Consistency ±30 min Same bedtime and wake time daily, weekends included. Regularity matters nearly as much as duration. Bedroom 65–68 °F Cool, dark, quiet. Core temperature has to drop for deep sleep to happen. What actually helps, in order of effect A fixed wake time. Anchor this first, even after a bad night. Your bedtime will follow within a week or two. No caffeine after ~2 pm. Caffeine has a half-life of 5–6 hours, so a 4 pm coffee still has a quarter of its dose active at midnight. You may fall asleep fine and still lose deep sleep. Dark and cool. Blackout curtains or a sleep mask. Even small amounts of light suppress melatonin. Dim lights and screens down 30–60 min before bed. Not because blue light is uniquely evil, but because bright light and stimulating content delay sleep onset. No large meals or alcohol within 2–3 hours. Alcohol is the worst offender — it puts you to sleep fast and then destroys the second half of the night. Get morning daylight within an hour of waking, 10 minutes outside. This is the strongest signal for setting your circadian clock, which is what determines when you can fall asleep at night. Don't train hard within 2 hours of bed if it leaves you wired. Some people are fine; if you're not, move the session earlier. Naps: 20 minutes, or 90 minutes, before 3 pm. The in-between length wakes you in deep sleep and leaves you groggy. If you sleep 6 hours a night, fix that before changing anything else about your training. Adding sets, buying creatine, or optimizing your macros while chronically under-slept is rearranging furniture in a burning house. This is the highest-leverage change available to most beginners and it costs nothing but scheduling.
records.k: What actually helps, in order of effect

records.t: You train Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. The other four days are not wasted — they are when the adaptation happens. What you do on them still matters. Do Why Walk 30–60 minutes Increases blood flow to sore muscles, aids clearance, near-zero recovery cost, helps keep a bulk lean. 10 minutes of mobility Joint health and range of motion improve with frequency, not intensity. See the routine . Easy skill practice (a few handstand kick-ups, a couple of hangs) Skills improve with frequent, low-fatigue exposure. This is not "extra training." Grease the groove — one easy assisted pull-up when you pass the bar Never near failure, never sore. Accelerates skill acquisition on the pull-up substantially. Eat and sleep normally Rest days are not lower-calorie days. Growth happens today. Don't add a "light" extra workout because you feel good The most common way beginners quietly overtrain. Recovery debt shows up two weeks later as a stall.

Delayed Onset Muscle Soreness peaks 24–48 hours after training, especially after new exercises or lots of eccentric work. It is a normal response to unfamiliar loading. It is not a measure of how good the workout was — experienced trainees making excellent progress are rarely very sore. DOMS (normal) Injury (stop) Where Spread through the belly of the muscle Sharp and pinpoint, usually at a joint or a tendon Timing Starts 12–24 h after, peaks at 24–48 h Often immediate, or during a specific movement Feel Dull ache, tight, tender to press Sharp, stabbing, burning, electric, or a pop With movement Improves as you warm up Stays the same or gets worse Symmetry Usually both sides equally Usually one side Duration Gone in 2–4 days Persists or recurs every session Swelling / bruising No Sometimes — always a red flag What to do Train anyway, maybe with fewer sets. Light movement helps. Stop that movement. See the traffic light . What actually reduces DOMS: gradual progression (the real answer), light movement, sleep, and adequate protein. What doesn't: static stretching before or after, and — despite how good it feels — most of what's sold as recovery gear. Ice baths reduce soreness but also blunt some of the adaptation signal, so they are the wrong tool while you're trying to build muscle. Severe soreness plus dark urine is a medical emergency. Extreme, disproportionate soreness (usually after a wildly excessive first session), swelling, weakness, and cola-colored urine can indicate rhabdomyolysis. Go to an emergency room. It is rare, but it happens specifically to enthusiastic beginners who do 300 push-ups on day one.

Green — keep training Muscle burn during a set General muscle ache for 1–3 days after Stiffness that warms out in 5 minutes Fatigue that goes away after a rest day Yellow — modify now A specific joint aches during one movement but not others Mild discomfort that's still there the next morning Pain at the very end of a range of motion Something that's been "a little off" for more than a week Do: drop back a rung, shorten the range, reduce sets, extend the warm-up, and swap in a pain-free variation of the same pattern. Do not push through and hope. Red — stop Sharp, stabbing, or electric pain Pain right on a joint line or a tendon Numbness or tingling down an arm or leg Anything that popped, and then hurt Visible swelling or bruising Pain that gets worse as you warm up Loss of strength or range of motion you can't explain Do: stop that movement entirely. Train everything else that's pain-free. If it isn't clearly improving within 7–10 days, see a physical therapist or a sports-medicine doctor. Early is cheap; late is not. The most useful principle in the whole injury section. An injury almost never means you should stop training — it means you should stop training that one movement . Sore elbow? Train legs and core. Tweaked knee? Train upper body. Continuing to train around an injury preserves the habit, keeps the rest of your body progressing, and generally improves the injured area's recovery through better circulation and less deconditioning.

records.h: Tendons, and why they lag behind muscle
records.t: Muscle adapts to training in weeks. Tendons, ligaments, and joint capsules adapt in months — they have far less blood supply and a much slower collagen turnover. That gap is why the classic calisthenics injury happens at month 4–8, not month 1: your muscles got strong enough to attempt something your connective tissue was never prepared for. What protects tendons: The rep gates in the ladders. They are deliberately conservative. Clearing 3×12 before moving on isn't about your muscles — it's about accumulating enough time under load for the tendon to remodel. Slow eccentrics. Controlled lowering is one of the best-evidenced tendon-strengthening stimuli there is. Isometric holds. Long holds (30–45 s) at moderate intensity build tendon stiffness and often reduce tendon pain immediately. Support holds, dead hangs, and L-sits do double duty here. Gradual, boring progression. Adding one rep per week is a tendon-friendly rate. Jumping two rungs because you felt strong is not. Full range of motion, which loads the tendon across its whole length rather than one spot. Not skipping warm-ups. Cold connective tissue is stiffer and injures more easily.

records.h: The five injuries you're most likely to get
records.t: 1 · Wrist pain most common Why: push-ups, planks, and handstands hold the wrist in deep extension under load — a position it never otherwise sees. Almost every beginner gets some version of this. Prevent: do the wrist prep sequence every single session. It is two minutes and it prevents most cases. Work around it: do push-ups on fists (neutral wrist), on parallettes or push-up handles, or on dumbbells. Reduce handstand volume. Spread your fingers and grip the floor rather than letting the weight sit on the heel of the hand. Rehab: gentle wrist flexion and extension against light resistance, progressive loaded wrist rocks, and forearm massage. Usually resolves in 2–4 weeks with prep plus modification. 2 · Elbow tendinopathy — golfer's or tennis elbow months 3–9 Why: too much straight-arm work too early (levers, planche attempts), a sudden jump in pull-up volume, or hanging with completely passive shoulders. Pain on the inside of the elbow is the medial (golfer's) version — the common one in calisthenics. Prevent: earn the front lever prerequisites before starting it. Warm up with band pull-aparts and light hangs. Don't double your pull volume in one week. Work around it: switch to a neutral or underhand grip, reduce range, cut volume by half. Rings, which let the elbow rotate freely, are usually more comfortable than a fixed bar. Rehab: slow, heavy-ish eccentric wrist curls (3×15, 4-second lowering, daily-ish) plus isometric holds. This has strong evidence behind it. Expect 6–12 weeks, and don't abandon the protocol the week it starts feeling better. 3 · Shoulder impingement / rotator cuff irritation Why: too much pressing relative to pulling, flared elbows in push-ups, dips going too deep, very wide-grip pull-ups, and generally weak scapular control. Prevent: match or exceed push volume with pull volume. Keep push-up elbows at 45°. Stop dips at parallel. Include band pull-aparts and face-pulls in every warm-up. Learn scapular retraction and depression. Work around it: narrow your grip, reduce depth, use a neutral grip, drop overhead work temporarily. Keep rowing — rowing usually helps. Rehab: external rotations with a light band, prone Y-T-W raises, scapular push-ups and scapular pulls, and serratus work (push-up plus). If there's night pain or you can't raise your arm overhead, get it looked at. 4 · Lower back pain Why: sagging hips in push-ups and planks, leg raises done with an arched lower back, and weak glutes forcing the erectors to do the hip's job. Prevent: brace properly — ribs down, pelvis slightly tucked, glutes squeezed — on every plank, push-up, and hollow hold. Never let the lower back arch off the floor during a hollow hold or leg raise; regress instead. Work around it: swap leg raises for dead bugs, hollow holds for tuck holds, and add glute bridges and bird dogs. Red flags — see a doctor: pain radiating down a leg, numbness or tingling, weakness in the foot, or any change in bladder or bowel function. 5 · Knee pain (usually patellofemoral) Why: jumping into pistol squats before the required ankle mobility and single-leg strength exist; knees caving inward; a large sudden jump in leg volume. Prevent: progress the squat ladder in order. Actively push the knee out over the second toe. Build ankle mobility with ankle rocks. Train hamstrings and glutes, not just quads. Work around it: reduce depth to a pain-free range, use box squats and split squats instead of deep single-leg work, and add glute bridges and hamstring work. Rehab: quad strengthening in a pain-free range, glute medius work (side-lying leg raises, banded walks), and ankle mobility. Knee pain that's worse going down stairs is the classic patellofemoral pattern.

records.t: Do this most days, ideally not immediately after training. Mobility responds to frequency, not intensity; ten minutes daily beats an hour once a week by a wide margin. Movement Dose Targets Deep squat hold (heels down, elbows pushing knees out) 2 × 60 s Ankles, hips, adductors — carries directly into pistol squats Couch stretch (rear foot up on a couch, half kneeling) 60 s /side Hip flexors and quads — undoes sitting all day 90/90 hip switches 10 /side Hip internal and external rotation Towel or band shoulder dislocates 2 × 10 Shoulder flexion — essential for handstands Thoracic extension over a rolled towel 10 reps Upper back extension, fixes rounded posture Cat-cow 10 reps Spinal segmentation Wrist rocks (all four directions) 10 each Wrist extension and flexion tolerance Jefferson curl with no weight, or a seated hamstring reach 5 slow reps Hamstrings and posterior chain — the L-sit limiter Ankle rocks against a wall 10 /side Ankle dorsiflexion

Type When Effect Dynamic — leg swings, arm circles, movement through a range Before training, always Raises tissue temperature and prepares the range you're about to use. No downside. Static — hold a stretch 30–60 s After training, or as a separate session Improves long-term flexibility. Long static holds immediately before max-effort work slightly reduce force output — so save them for after. Loaded stretching — deep squat holds, Jefferson curls, weighted stretches Separate sessions The most effective way to build usable range, because you gain strength in the new range rather than just tolerance. Foam rolling Anytime Temporarily reduces perceived soreness and increases range for ~10 minutes. Pleasant, low-cost, no lasting structural change. Fine to do; don't expect much. Stretching does not prevent injury or reduce soreness — that's a long-standing myth. Stretch because you want more range of motion (which you do — handstands, deep squats, and L-sits all demand it), not as injury insurance. Progressive, well-managed loading is the actual injury insurance.

Fatigue accumulates faster than you perceive it. A deload every 6 weeks is scheduled into the program — half the sets, 4–5 RIR, keep the skill work. Take an unscheduled one whenever two or more of these are true for a week: Reps declining across multiple exercises Joints aching before the warm-up even starts Resting heart rate up 5+ bpm Sleep getting worse despite being tired Motivation dropping for sessions you normally enjoy Getting sick more often than usual

True clinical overtraining syndrome is rare and takes months of serious abuse to reach. Overreaching — doing more than you're currently recovering from — is common and easy to fix. Watch for: Physical Performance dropping for 2+ weeks despite consistent effort Soreness that never fully clears Elevated resting heart rate Frequent minor illnesses Nagging aches in multiple joints at once Loss of appetite Mental Dreading sessions you used to look forward to Irritability, low mood, poor concentration Sleep getting worse the more tired you get Feeling like you need to do more because results stalled The fix is almost always the same: one deload week, then return at 75% of the previous volume and rebuild over three weeks. Not a full week off, not a program change, and definitely not more volume.

Your body doesn't have separate recovery budgets for exams, a bad week at work, family stress, and squats. It has one. Chronically elevated cortisol from life stress directly impairs recovery, reduces protein synthesis, degrades sleep quality, and increases injury risk — through exactly the same pathways as excessive training. Practically: during a genuinely stressful stretch, reduce training volume by about a third rather than trying to power through. Keep the three sessions — the habit and the mood benefit are real — but drop a set from each exercise and stay further from failure. You'll maintain almost everything, and you'll come out the other side able to push again. Trying to set records during finals week is how people get hurt and quit. records.t: Everything in Phase 1 of the program runs on this list. Do not delay starting because you don't have equipment yet. Item Used for Notes Floor Push-ups, planks, hollow holds, squats, dead bugs, bridges Carpet or a rug is easier on wrists and elbows than tile. Two sturdy chairs Bench dips, incline push-ups, Bulgarian split squats, elevated pike push-ups Test that they don't slide or tip before you put weight on them. Push them against a wall. A solid dining table Inverted rows — the single most valuable free substitute you have Grip the edge, lie underneath, pull your chest to it. Check it can hold your weight and can't tip; weigh the far side down if needed. Stairs Incline push-ups at any height, deficit calf raises, step-ups The most adjustable free equipment in your house. Two towels on a hard floor Sliding leg curls, mountain climbers, slide-out planks Only works on hardwood, tile, or laminate. A phone Rest timer, filming your form, logging sets Filming one set from the side every two weeks is free coaching.

This is the highest-return money you will spend on fitness, probably ever. In priority order: # Item Typical price Why What to look for 1 Doorway pull-up bar search → $25–40 The one purchase that changes everything. Vertical pulling has no good floor substitute, and lats are the biggest muscle in your upper body. Leverage-mount (over-the-door frame) type, 300 lb rating, multiple grip positions including neutral, and padded foam where it contacts the frame. Full comparison below. 2 Resistance band set (loop / pull-up assist bands) search → $20–35 Assisted pull-ups, band pull-aparts, face pulls, Pallof presses, external rotations. The shoulder-health work in every warm-up needs one. A set of 3–5 continuous loop bands of different thicknesses (not the tube-with-handles kind). Get at least one heavy band for pull-up assistance and one light band for warm-ups. 3 Exercise mat search → $20–30 Saves your spine on leg raises and hollow holds, your knees on split squats, and your elbows on planks. Also defines a "training space," which matters more psychologically than it sounds. 1/2" thick, at least 24" × 68". NBR or TPE foam. A thin yoga mat is not enough padding for floor core work. 4 Digital kitchen scale search → $10–15 You cannot hit 2,800 calories and 150 g of protein reliably by eyeballing. Two weeks with a scale calibrates your estimates permanently. Grams and ounces, tare function, 11 lb capacity. Any cheap one works. 5 Bathroom scale search → $15–25 Daily weigh-ins are the primary feedback loop for whether you're eating enough. 0.2 lb increments. Ignore the "body fat %" feature on cheap scales — bioimpedance from feet only is close to useless. 6 Cloth tape measure search → $6–10 Monthly measurements catch progress the scale hides. See the measurement protocol . A flexible cloth or fiberglass tape with inches. The spring-loaded "body tape" versions that apply constant tension are worth the extra couple of dollars for consistency. Highest weight rating. Permanent. Requires drilling into studs or joists and a landlord who won't mind. Best if you own the place. Great if you have the space and budget. Park bar / playground Free Free, full range, usually has dip bars and rings nearby, and training outside is genuinely good for adherence. Weather. Travel time. Not always available at 6 am. Use it if it's close. Before you hang from anything, check three things. (1) The door frame: the trim must be solidly attached to the framing behind it, not just tacked to drywall. Push hard on it. (2) The weight rating must exceed your bodyweight with a wide margin — 300 lb minimum at 150 lb, because dynamic loading during a rep can be several times your static weight. (3) Test it slowly: hang with your feet still on the ground and gradually shift weight onto it before you commit. Do this test every time you reinstall the bar. And keep the floor under it clear.

records.h: Tier 2 — months 3–6, once you've earned it
records.t: Buy these when the program actually calls for them, not up front. Nothing here is necessary before month 3. Item Price Unlocks What to look for Parallettes search → $30–60 L-sits, deficit push-ups, tuck planche work, handstand work on a neutral wrist, and dips if they're tall enough. Extremely versatile for the price. Low ones (6–8") for L-sits and planche work; tall ones (12–24") if you also want dips. Wooden dowels are kinder on the hands than steel. Check they don't tip sideways. Gymnastic rings search → $30–50 Ring rows, ring dips, ring push-ups, support holds, and eventually the front lever and muscle-up. The single most versatile piece of equipment in calisthenics. 1.1" wood rings with long numbered straps and cam buckles. Wood grips better and is warmer than plastic. You need somewhere to hang them: a pull-up bar, a tree branch, a beam, or a park frame. Dip station / parallel bars search → $60–120 Real dips (much better than bench dips), L-sits, and support holds. Adjustable height, wide stable base, 400+ lb rating. Set the bars just wider than your shoulders. Some doorway bars convert into a floor dip station — check before buying separately. Weighted vest or dip belt search → $40–120 The cleanest way to progress once you can do 10+ pull-ups or 15+ dips. Beats hunting for ever more exotic variations. Adjustable in small increments (2.5–5 lb). A dip belt plus plates is cheaper and more precise; a vest is more convenient and works for push-ups and squats too. A backpack with books does 80% of this for free. Ab wheel search → $12–25 One of the best anti-extension core exercises there is, and very cheap. Wide wheel or dual wheels for stability. Start from the knees with a short range — it is much harder than it looks. Door anchor for bands search → $8–15 Face pulls, Pallof presses, band rows, and external rotations at any angle. Foam ball or thick padded type so it can't pull through the door. Furniture sliders search → $8–15 Sliding leg curls, slide-out planks, reverse lunges — works on carpet, where towels don't. Get the double-sided kind (hard side for carpet, felt side for hard floors).

Item Price Worth it? Liquid chalk search → $10–15 Yes, if your grip slips before your back fails. Liquid chalk over block chalk indoors — far less mess. Foam roller search → $20–35 Feels good, temporarily improves range, doesn't change anything structurally. Nice, not necessary. Massage / lacrosse ball search → $5–10 Better than a foam roller for pecs, glutes, and feet, and a tenth of the price. Wrist wraps search → $12–20 Useful for handstand volume if your wrists complain. Not a substitute for wrist prep — that's the actual fix. Adjustable dumbbells search → $100–300 If you want to fill the hamstring, calf, and rear-delt gaps properly, or add load precisely. Not calisthenics, but nobody gets a prize for purity. Yoga blocks search → $12–20 Improvised parallettes, elevation for stretches, hand support in the deep squat. Gym timer / interval app Free Yes. Timing rests properly is one of the easy wins.

Item Why not Pressure-mount tension pull-up bars Genuine fall risk. They rely on friction and loosen over time. Not worth saving $10. "Push-up boards" with color-coded holes Solves a problem you don't have. Hand position isn't what's limiting you. Ab belts, vibrating plates, EMS devices Do nothing. There is no passive route to muscle. Grip strengtheners (spring type) Dead hangs and pull-ups build far more usable grip than a spring gripper. Weight-loss teas, waist trainers, sauna suits Water loss theater. Expensive branded programs and apps The whole program is on this site . Beginner programming is not the scarce resource — consistency is. Barefoot-style "training" shoes, day one You're training on the floor. Go barefoot or wear socks. Buy shoes when you have a reason.

Train barefoot or in socks for indoor calisthenics. Better proprioception, and for pistol squats and handstands a flat foot on the ground is what you want. Running shoes with a soft, elevated heel are actively unhelpful for squatting. If you want shoes: flat, thin, firm sole — trainers, court shoes, or minimalist shoes. Not running shoes. Fitted shirts or none. A loose shirt gets caught under your hands during push-ups and hides the form issues you're trying to see on video. Shorts you can squat deeply in without restriction. Long sleeves for bar work in cold weather — cold tissue is stiffer and more injury-prone.

Food tracking MyFitnessPal (biggest database), Cronometer (best micronutrient detail), MacroFactor (best at adjusting your target automatically). Free tiers cover everything you need. Rest timer Your phone's built-in timer, or any free interval-timer app. Form check Your phone camera plus a way to prop it up. Slow-motion mode is useful for tempo. Weight trend smoothing Any app that shows a moving average, or a spreadsheet with a 7-day rolling average column. Never judge on a single day.

records.h: The free option: use a park
records.t: Most public parks and school playgrounds have a pull-up bar, and many US cities now have dedicated calisthenics or "fitness court" setups with bars at multiple heights, parallel bars, and sometimes rings. That is a complete gym for $0. Search for "calisthenics park near me" or check the map at calisthenics-parks.com , a community-maintained worldwide directory. Practical notes: bring liquid chalk if the bars are slick, wear gloves or long sleeves in winter because cold steel is genuinely painful, go early or late if you're self-conscious (nobody is watching, but it takes a few weeks to believe that), and have an indoor fallback session for weather so the habit never breaks.

$0 — the honest minimum Floor, chairs, table, towel, backpack full of books, and a nearby park bar if you have one. Gets you: all of Phase 1 and most of Phase 2. Genuinely enough for 3–6 months of real progress. The gap is vertical pulling, which the park bar closes entirely. $60 — the smart start Doorway pull-up bar ($30) + resistance band set ($25) + tape measure ($8). Gets you: every pattern in the program, properly, through month 6. If you buy one thing on this page, buy this combination. $250 — the full home setup Tier 1 in full ($130) + rings ($40) + parallettes ($45) + ab wheel ($20) + door anchor ($12). Gets you: two to three years of progression without ever needing a gym, including rings work, L-sits, front lever training, and muscle-up practice. Previous ← Recovery Next The tracker →

Can you actually build real muscle with just bodyweight? Yes. Muscle responds to mechanical tension close to failure, and it cannot tell whether that tension comes from a barbell or from your own bodyweight at a bad leverage. Research comparing bodyweight training to weight training with equated effort and proximity to failure finds similar hypertrophy. Where bodyweight training genuinely struggles is fine-grained loading — you can't add 5 lb, so you have to jump between variations — and legs , where bodyweight stops being challenging quickly. Both are solvable: use the five levers , go single-leg, and add a loaded backpack when you outgrow a variation. How long until I see results? Week 1–2: soreness, then it fades. Nothing visible. Week 3–4: reps climbing noticeably. That's your nervous system, not new muscle. Week 6–8: you start to notice small changes — usually shoulders, arms, and posture. Nobody else does yet. Week 10–14: other people start commenting. This is the classic "have you been working out?" window. Month 6: obvious to anyone who knew you before. Month 12: a genuinely different body, if you ate and slept for it. I'm 5'9" and 150 lb. Am I too skinny for this? You're at an ideal starting point, and specifically a better one than someone heavier. Calisthenics is a strength-to-weight sport: every movement in it is easier at lower bodyweight. A lighter person gets their first pull-up, dip, and handstand far sooner, which means more early wins, which means they don't quit. Your BMI is 22.1 — squarely healthy. You are not underweight; you are under-muscled, which is a training and eating problem, not a weight problem. Trying to fix it by just getting on a scale-driven bulk without training would only add fat. Will lifting or calisthenics stunt my growth if I'm a teenager? No. This is a persistent myth with no support in the evidence. Major sports-medicine bodies — including the American Academy of Pediatrics — endorse resistance training for adolescents, noting improvements in strength, bone density, body composition, and injury resistance. Growth plates are damaged by acute trauma (a fall, a bad landing, a maximal lift with terrible form), not by well-supervised progressive training. Bodyweight training is a particularly safe entry point because the load is inherently capped at your own weight. Use good form, progress gradually, don't chase 1-rep maxes, and don't train through joint pain — the same advice that applies to adults. How much does genetics actually matter? It matters a lot for your ceiling and your rate, and almost not at all for whether this is worth doing. Muscle fiber type, tendon insertions, limb lengths, and hormone levels vary widely, and studies of identical training programs consistently find some people gain three times as much as others. What genetics does not determine is whether you'll be dramatically stronger and better-built in two years than you are today. Essentially everyone who trains consistently and eats for it gets that. Limb length also cuts both ways in calisthenics: long arms make pull-ups harder but levers easier; short limbs are the reverse.

records.t: I can't do a single pull-up. What do I do? Completely normal — most untrained beginners can't. Run all three of these in the same week: Negatives. Jump or step to the top, lower for 5 seconds. 3 sets of 5. Builds the top half of the movement. Band- or foot-assisted full reps. Teaches you to pull from a dead hang, which negatives never do. Rows and scapular pull-ups. Your mid-back initiates the pull, and it's usually the weak link. Also: start with chin-ups (underhand). They're meaningfully easier because the biceps contribute more, and most people get a chin-up 2–4 weeks before a pull-up. Expect 4–12 weeks to your first rep from a true zero. Should I train every day? Can I do more than 3 days? You can eventually, but not now. Three full-body days with rest between them hits every muscle 3×/week — near-optimal frequency — while giving unconditioned tendons the recovery they need. Adding days as a beginner produces more fatigue, not more growth, and it's the most common route to a month-4 injury. What you can do daily: walk, do the 10-minute mobility routine , practice handstands briefly, and grease the groove with one easy pull-up rep in passing. None of that is "a workout," and none of it costs meaningful recovery. Is the "100 push-ups a day" type of challenge worth doing? As a challenge, sure — it builds a habit and it's fun. As a training program, no. Doing the same easy exercise for high reps every day means no progressive overload, no recovery, one movement pattern, and nothing for your back or legs. You end up good at push-ups and imbalanced everywhere else, often with cranky shoulders. If the daily-challenge format is what gets you to show up, use it for the first month to build the habit, then switch to the actual program . High reps or low reps for muscle? Anything from about 5 to about 30 reps builds similar muscle if you take the set close to failure . That's the key qualifier. 6–12 is the practical sweet spot: enough tension to build strength, not so many reps that the set becomes a cardiovascular event. In calisthenics the real signal is different: if you're over ~20 reps, the exercise has stopped being a strength stimulus and you should change a lever. If you're under 5, it's too hard — regress. Do I need to feel sore for it to have worked? No. Soreness reflects novelty and eccentric damage, not effectiveness. You'll be sore in weeks 1–2, sore again whenever you introduce a new movement, and then mostly not sore even while making your best progress. Experienced trainees who are growing well are rarely very sore. Judge your training by whether the numbers in your log are going up. That's the only reliable indicator. Should I train if I'm still sore? Usually yes. Light-to-moderate training on sore muscles typically reduces soreness through increased blood flow, and it doesn't impair recovery. Cut a set or two if you need to. Exceptions: if the soreness is severe enough to change your form, train a different pattern that day. And if it's sharp, joint-located, or one-sided, it isn't soreness — check the pain traffic light . How do I build legs without weights? Go single-leg. Splitting the load onto one leg roughly doubles the demand, and adds a big balance and stabilizer tax on top. The ladder — split squat → Bulgarian split squat → box pistol → shrimp squat → pistol squat — provides years of progression at 150 lb. Then add the two things everyone forgets: hamstrings (sliding leg curls, Nordic negatives, single-leg RDLs — squats barely touch them) and calves (single-leg raises off a stair, high reps). A loaded backpack extends all of it further. If you eventually want serious leg size, a pair of adjustable dumbbells is the honest answer — nobody gives out prizes for equipment purity. Can I mix calisthenics with weights or running? Yes. They aren't opposing religions. Adding dumbbell work for hamstrings, rear delts, and calves fills the exact gaps calisthenics leaves. Running is good for your heart and recovery capacit

records.t: How do I get visible abs? Two independent things, and only one is training. (1) Build the muscle — hollow holds, leg raises, ab wheel, L-sits, and heavy compound work all thicken the abdominal wall. (2) Reduce the body fat covering it — that is entirely a nutrition outcome. Visible abs typically appear around 10–12% body fat for men and 18–20% for women. There is no such thing as spot reduction: you cannot choose where fat comes off, and crunches don't burn abdominal fat. At 150 lb and lean-ish, you are likely close enough that building the muscle is the higher-leverage half — which is also convenient, because it's the half that's compatible with bulking. Can I build muscle and lose fat at the same time? Yes, in specific circumstances, and you happen to be in one of them: complete beginners, people returning after a layoff, and people with higher body fat can all recomposition at maintenance calories with high protein. That said, at your body composition it's the slower path. You have room to add muscle, so a lean bulk will get you further in the same time. Recomp is the right answer if you're starting at higher body fat. How do I get the V-taper / wide back look? Lats and rear delts, plus a waist that doesn't grow much. That means pull-ups above everything else , plus rows, plus keeping the bulk lean so the waist stays put. Wide-grip pull-ups are not the secret — they shorten the range and stress the shoulder without building a wider back any faster. Full-range pull-ups with progressively more load is the actual answer. What about my grip? My hands hurt and I'm getting calluses. Calluses are normal and useful — they're protective. Keep them filed down flat with a pumice stone or file after a shower. Thick raised calluses are what tear off mid-set, which is genuinely painful and costs you a week of hanging. If grip fails before your back does, add dead hangs at the end of every session, and use liquid chalk. Skip lifting straps for now — grip strength is worth having, and pull-ups build it for free.

records.t: I live in an apartment. Will this annoy my neighbors? Calisthenics is close to the quietest strength training there is — no plates, no dropping anything. Two things make noise: jumping (jump squats, jumping jacks, kick-ups landing hard) and a doorway pull-up bar knocking against the frame. Fixes: swap jumping jacks for marching or step-jacks in the warm-up, land handstand kick-ups softly (which you should be doing anyway for control), train on a mat, and pad the pull-up bar contact points with a folded towel. What time of day should I train? The time you'll actually do it, consistently, for months. Strength does peak slightly in the late afternoon for most people, but the effect is small enough to be irrelevant next to the effect of skipping sessions. Whatever you pick, keep it constant — it makes the habit automatic, and it makes your session-to-session numbers comparable. Home or park? Both. A park with a pull-up bar and parallel bars is a free, better gym — bars at proper height, full headroom, and being outside genuinely helps adherence for a lot of people. Home is weather-proof and has zero travel friction. The best setup: a doorway bar at home as your default, and a park session when the weather's good. Always have an indoor fallback so a rainy week never breaks the habit. Should I take creatine? Is it safe? Creatine monohydrate is the most-studied sports supplement in existence, with decades of safety data in healthy people. It reliably improves performance in repeated high-effort sets by a few percent, which compounds over months. 5 g a day, any time, no loading phase needed. Buy plain monohydrate — the "advanced" forms are marketing. It does cause a couple of pounds of water retention inside the muscle, which is harmless but will show on the scale in week one — don't misread that as fat. If you're under 18, run it past a parent or doctor first; the safety data is mostly in adults, and it is genuinely optional. Fix sleep, calories, protein, and consistency first — those matter 50× more. Do I need to do cardio? For muscle, no. For health, recovery capacity, and not being winded between sets, yes — and it's cheap. Two or three easy 25–40 minute sessions a week (brisk walking counts) plus generally walking a lot covers it without eating into your surplus or your recovery. Skip long runs and high-volume intervals while you're bulking. See the cardio section .

records.t: How do I stay motivated? You don't — motivation is a feeling and feelings are unreliable. Build systems that work when motivation is absent: Fixed days and a fixed time , in your calendar as recurring events. Remove the decision. Lower the activation cost. Mat out, bar up, clothes ready. Most skipped sessions die in the first two minutes. Track everything. Watching numbers climb is the most durable motivator there is, and it's the one that survives a bad mood. Set process goals, not outcome goals. "Three sessions this week" is entirely in your control; "gain 10 lb" is not. Never miss twice. One missed session is noise. Two in a row is how a habit dies. Show up short. On bad days do the 20-minute minimum session . Preserving the streak is worth more than the workout. I missed three weeks. Did I lose everything? No. Meaningful muscle loss takes considerably longer than three weeks of inactivity, and what you do lose comes back much faster than it was built — muscle memory is a real, well-documented phenomenon involving retained nuclei in the muscle fibers. Come back at the same rungs with 2–3 sets instead of 4, expect real soreness for one week, and you'll be back where you were within two to three weeks. The thing you actually lost is habit momentum — so restart today , not on Monday. I feel self-conscious training in public. Everyone at a park bar was once unable to do a pull-up, and the ones who are good at it are unusually likely to be encouraging about it. In practice people are almost entirely occupied with themselves. Practical steps: go at off-peak hours at first, wear headphones, have your session written down so you never look lost, and give it three visits. It stops mattering fast.

records.t: The myth What's actually true "Bodyweight training only builds endurance, not size." Muscle responds to tension near failure regardless of its source. Use hard variations in the 5–15 rep range and you build size. "Spot reduction — crunches burn belly fat." Fat is mobilized systemically. You cannot choose where it leaves from. Abs come from building the muscle and lowering overall body fat. "Toning is a different kind of training." "Toned" means muscle plus low enough body fat to see it. There is no separate toning stimulus — it's the same training. "Muscle turns into fat if you stop." Different tissues entirely; neither converts to the other. Stopping means muscle atrophies and, if you keep eating the same, fat accumulates. Two processes, not one. "You must eat protein within 30 minutes of training." The elevated protein-synthesis response lasts many hours. Total daily protein and its distribution across meals are what matter. "Lifting stunts teenage growth." Not supported by evidence. Properly progressed resistance training is endorsed for adolescents and improves bone density. "No pain, no gain." Effort, yes. Joint pain, no. Training through the wrong kind of pain converts a two-week annoyance into a six-month problem. "More sweat means a better workout." Sweat reflects temperature and humidity, not stimulus. A heavy set of pull-ups in a cold room builds more muscle than an hour of sweaty circuits. "You need to confuse the muscle with constant variety." Muscles respond to progressive tension, not novelty. Constant switching prevents both loading and tracking. "Rest days are for people who aren't serious." Adaptation happens on rest days. Training without them just accumulates fatigue and injury risk. "Carbs at night make you fat." Total daily calories determine fat gain. Timing has a negligible effect. A pre-bed protein-and-carb meal is genuinely useful. "Sit-ups give you a six-pack." They train hip flexors more than abs and don't touch body fat. Hollow holds, leg raises, and ab wheel rollouts are far better ab exercises. "Stretching before training prevents injury." Static stretching before max effort slightly reduces force output and doesn't prevent injury. Warm up dynamically; stretch afterward or separately. "You have to go to failure every set." Sets at 1–3 RIR produce nearly identical growth with far less fatigue and injury risk. Failure is a tool, not a default. "Deep dips and behind-the-neck pulls build more muscle." They mostly build shoulder problems. Range of motion is good up to the point where the joint leaves a safe position.

References Where the claims on this site come from Fitness advice is mostly repeated, rarely sourced. This page lists the research behind the specific numbers used here — volume targets, protein ceilings, sleep, tendon adaptation — plus an honest account of what the evidence doesn't settle, and where this site quietly assumes you're a young adult male. Read this before you read the list. These are named by author, year, title, and journal so you can find them yourself — search links go to PubMed. Deliberately no DOIs or page numbers, because a citation detail that's slightly wrong is worse than one you had to look up. If a number here matters to a decision you're making, read the actual paper: study populations, training status, and effect sizes matter more than the headline. And nothing here is medical advice. Most of what circulates as fitness advice is one of three things: an extrapolation from a mechanism ("X raises Y in a test tube, therefore X builds muscle"), a single small study, or somebody's successful personal routine. All three are weak. A rough hierarchy, strongest first: Meta-analyses and systematic reviews of randomized trials — pools many studies, so noise averages out. Still only as good as the studies inside it. Randomized controlled trials in the relevant population. Watch the training status of the subjects: results from untrained beginners often don't transfer to trained lifters, and vice versa. Observational studies — can show associations, cannot establish cause. Mechanistic and acute studies — measure a signal (protein synthesis over 4 hours, a hormone spike) that may or may not translate into muscle months later. This is where most supplement marketing lives. Expert practice and coaching consensus — genuinely useful where research is thin, which is most of skill progression. Label it as what it is. Anecdote and personal routines — near-zero evidential weight, high entertainment value. Three habits that will save you from most bad advice: Ask about effect size, not just significance. "Statistically significant" can mean a 1% difference. Many real effects are too small to matter next to consistency. Ask who was studied. Trained vs. untrained, young vs. old, male vs. female, calorie surplus vs. deficit. These change results dramatically. Expect individual variation. Studies of identical programs consistently find some participants gaining several times what others do. Group averages tell you where to start, not what you'll get.

This is the claim the whole site rests on, so it's worth being precise. The strong version — "bodyweight training is equivalent to weight training" — is not established. What is reasonably supported: Progressive push-up training produces strength and muscle-thickness gains comparable to bench pressing when load and progression are matched. Kotarsky, Christensen, Miller & Hackney (2018), Effect of progressive calisthenic push-up training on muscle strength and thickness , Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. find → Load per se matters much less than proximity to failure (the low- vs. high-load meta-analysis above), which is the mechanism that lets bodyweight work at all. Calisthenics training improves strength, posture, and body composition against non-training controls. Thomas, Bianco, Paoli & Palma (2017), The relation between calisthenics training, posture, strength and body composition , Isokinetics and Exercise Science. Small trial, non-elite population — suggestive rather than decisive. find → Where bodyweight training is genuinely at a disadvantage, and where the site says so: fine-grained load progression, and lower-body loading past the point where single-leg variations stop being hard. Neither has much dedicated research — that's a mechanical argument, not an empirical one, and it's labelled as such on the start page .

Claim on this site Primary source Protein benefits plateau around 1.6 g/kg (≈0.73 g/lb). The site's 1.0 g/lb target is deliberately above the plateau, for margin. ( Nutrition §protein ) Morton et al. (2018), A systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength in healthy adults , British Journal of Sports Medicine. find → Roughly 0.4 g/kg of protein per meal across four meals is a sensible distribution target. ( Nutrition §protein ) Schoenfeld & Aragon (2018), How much protein can the body use in a single meal for muscle-building? Implications for daily protein distribution , Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition; Areta et al. (2013), Timing and distribution of protein ingestion during prolonged recovery from resistance exercise alters myofibrillar protein synthesis , Journal of Physiology. find → Gaining ~0.25–0.5% of bodyweight per week maximizes the muscle-to-fat ratio of a bulk. ( Nutrition §rate ) Iraki, Fitschen, Espinar & Helms (2019), Nutrition recommendations for bodybuilders in the off-season: a narrative review , Sports; Garthe et al. (2013), Effect of nutritional intervention on body composition and performance in elite athletes , European Journal of Sport Science. find → Pre-sleep protein supports overnight muscle protein synthesis. ( Nutrition §timing ) Res et al. (2012), Protein ingestion before sleep improves postexercise overnight recovery , Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise; Snijders et al. (2015), Protein ingestion before sleep increases muscle mass and strength gains during prolonged resistance-type exercise training , Journal of Nutrition. find → The "anabolic window" is far wider than 30 minutes. ( Nutrition §timing ) Aragon & Schoenfeld (2013), Nutrient timing revisited: is there a post-exercise anabolic window? , Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition. find → Beginners and returnees can gain muscle and lose fat simultaneously. ( FAQ , Nutrition §cut ) Barakat, Bell, Escalante & Stanton (2020), Body recomposition: can trained individuals build muscle and lose fat at the same time? , Strength and Conditioning Journal. find → The Mifflin–St Jeor equation is the basis of the calorie calculator. ( Nutrition §calculator ) Mifflin, St Jeor et al. (1990), A new predictive equation for resting energy expenditure in healthy individuals , American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. find → The Navy circumference method behind the body-fat estimator. ( Goals §tape ) Hodgdon & Beckett (1984), Prediction of percent body fat for U.S. Navy men and women from body circumferences and height , Naval Health Research Center technical reports. find → Alcohol suppresses post-exercise muscle protein synthesis. ( Nutrition §alcohol ) Parr et al. (2014), Alcohol ingestion impairs maximal post-exercise rates of myofibrillar protein synthesis following a single bout of concurrent training , PLoS ONE. find →

Claim on this site Primary source Creatine monohydrate improves performance in repeated high-effort work and has a strong long-term safety record in healthy people. ( Nutrition §supplements ) Kreider et al. (2017), International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: safety and efficacy of creatine supplementation in exercise, sport, and medicine , JISSN. find → Caffeine improves training performance and reduces perceived exertion. Guest et al. (2021), International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand: caffeine and exercise performance , JISSN. find → Protein powder is convenience, not a distinct effect beyond hitting total daily protein. Morton et al. (2018), above. BCAAs add nothing when total protein is adequate. Wolfe (2017), Branched-chain amino acids and muscle protein synthesis in humans: myth or reality? , JISSN. find → Vitamin D deficiency is common and is associated with impaired muscle function. Owens, Allison & Close (2018), Vitamin D and the athlete: current perspectives and new challenges , Sports Medicine. find →

Claim on this site Primary source Sleeping under 8 hours substantially increases injury risk in young athletes — the source of the "roughly doubles" figure. ( Recovery §sleep ) Milewski et al. (2014), Chronic lack of sleep is associated with increased sports injuries in adolescent athletes , Journal of Pediatric Orthopaedics. find → Sleep restriction shifts weight loss away from fat and toward lean mass, and worsens body-composition outcomes. Nedeltcheva et al. (2010), Insufficient sleep undermines dietary efforts to reduce adiposity , Annals of Internal Medicine. find → One week of restricted sleep measurably lowers testosterone in healthy young men. Leproult & Van Cauter (2011), Effect of 1 week of sleep restriction on testosterone levels in young healthy men , JAMA. find → Cold-water immersion blunts long-term strength and hypertrophy adaptation — why the site says not to ice-bath while building. ( Recovery §DOMS ) Roberts et al. (2015), Post-exercise cold water immersion attenuates acute anabolic signalling and long-term adaptations in muscle to strength training , Journal of Physiology. find → Psychological stress impairs recovery from strenuous exercise. ( Recovery §stress ) Stults-Kolehmainen & Bartholomew (2012), Psychological stress impairs short-term muscular recovery from resistance exercise , Medicine & Science in Sports & Exercise. find →

Claim on this site Primary source Tendon adapts far more slowly than muscle — the reason for conservative rep gates. ( Recovery §tendons ) Bohm, Mersmann & Arampatzis (2015), Human tendon adaptation in response to mechanical loading: a systematic review and meta-analysis , Sports Medicine – Open; Magnusson, Langberg & Kjaer (2010), The pathogenesis of tendinopathy in athletes: balancing the response to loading , Nature Reviews Rheumatology. find → Heavy slow eccentric loading is effective for tendinopathy — the basis of the elbow rehab protocol. ( Recovery §injuries ) Alfredson et al. (1998), Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis , American Journal of Sports Medicine; Cook & Purdam (2009), Is tendon pathology a continuum? , British Journal of Sports Medicine. find → Isometric holds can reduce tendon pain and are useful loading. Rio et al. (2015), Isometric exercise induces analgesia and reduces inhibition in patellar tendinopathy , British Journal of Sports Medicine. find → Gradual load progression is the main modifiable injury risk factor — sudden spikes in training load predict injury. Gabbett (2016), The training–injury prevention paradox: should athletes be training smarter and harder? , British Journal of Sports Medicine. find →

Myth Evidence Spot reduction: ab exercises burn belly fat Vispute et al. (2011), The effect of abdominal exercise on abdominal fat , Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research; Ramírez-Campillo et al. (2013), Regional fat changes induced by localized muscle endurance resistance training , JSCR. find → Stretching prevents soreness Herbert, de Noronha & Kamper (2011), Stretching to prevent or reduce muscle soreness after exercise , Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews. find → Static stretching before training is a good warm-up Simic, Sarabon & Markovic (2013), Does pre-exercise static stretching inhibit maximal muscular performance? A meta-analytical review , Scandinavian Journal of Medicine & Science in Sports; Behm et al. (2016), Acute effects of muscle stretching on physical performance, range of motion, and injury incidence in healthy active individuals: a systematic review , Applied Physiology, Nutrition, and Metabolism. find → Soreness indicates a good workout Damas et al. (2018), Muscle damage: current knowledge and controversies , and related work showing muscle damage is not required for, and does not track with, hypertrophy. find → Carbs at night make you fat No mechanism and no supporting trial evidence at matched calories; see Aragon & Schoenfeld above and the ISSN diet-and-body-composition position stand. find →

The claim that resistance training stunts growth has no support in the literature, and the major position statements say so explicitly: Stricker, Faigenbaum & McCambridge / AAP Council on Sports Medicine and Fitness (2020), Resistance training for children and adolescents , Pediatrics. find → Faigenbaum et al. (2009), Youth resistance training: updated position statement paper from the National Strength and Conditioning Association , Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. find → Lloyd et al. (2014), Position statement on youth resistance training: the 2014 International Consensus , British Journal of Sports Medicine. find → Growth-plate injuries in youth resistance training are rare and are associated with unsupervised maximal lifting and poor technique — not with progressive, well-coached training. Bodyweight training is a particularly low-risk entry point because the load is capped at your own weight.

records.h: What the evidence does not settle
records.t: Plenty of what's on this site is coaching consensus rather than research. It is presented as guidance because it works in practice, but you should know which is which: On this site Status The specific rep gates on each ladder (3×12 before moving up, etc.) Coaching convention. No study establishes these thresholds. They are deliberately conservative to buy tendon adaptation time. The exact ordering of progressions within a ladder Consensus and biomechanics. Broadly agreed among coaches; individual leverages change the difficulty order. Deloading every 6 weeks Practice, weakly supported. Fatigue management is real; the 6-week interval is a convention, not a finding. "1–2 lb of muscle per month in year one" Practitioner models (Alan Aragon's and Lyle McDonald's rate-of-gain models), widely used, not derived from a single trial. Individual variation is large. Skill practice done fresh and short of failure Motor-learning theory and gymnastics practice. Sound reasoning, thin sport-specific evidence. The specific strength standards table Widely circulated gym benchmarks, not normative population data. Use as a map, not a verdict. Push:pull volume ratios for shoulder health Clinical reasoning and coaching consensus. Plausible and low-cost; not established by trials. Optimal handstand teaching progressions Gymnastics coaching tradition. Effective in practice; essentially unstudied.

records.h: Who this site assumes you are
records.t: Every number here was set for one specific person: a healthy male in his late teens or twenties, 5'9", 150 lb, untrained, uninjured, training at home three days a week. That's useful precision, and it's also a bias worth naming. Here's what changes if that isn't you. If you're… What stays the same What changes Female Every exercise, every progression, the program structure, progressive overload, and the training principles. All of it. Calorie and BMR numbers (the calculator handles this ), body-fat reference ranges, and the upper-body strength standards. See below . Over 35 Program structure, exercises, progression logic. Longer warm-ups, slower connective-tissue adaptation, more recovery between hard sessions, and higher protein. See below . Under 16 Training is safe and beneficial; bodyweight is an ideal entry point. Emphasize technique over load, sleep 8–10 hours, skip supplements including creatine without a doctor's input, and expect that some of your progress is growth rather than training. Heavier than 150 lb Everything, but the ladders will take longer. Pull-ups and dips are meaningfully harder — you're lifting more. Spend longer on regressions; that's not failure, it's physics. If you're above roughly 20% body fat, a short cut first makes every movement easier. Carrying an injury Nothing — get an assessment first. This site cannot tell you which movements are safe for your specific injury. A physical therapist can, in one appointment, and it's worth the money. Already trained The reference material and the ladders above your current rung. The beginner rate-of-gain figures, the 24-week timeline, and the volume ramp are all too conservative for you.

Almost nothing about the training changes. Muscle physiology is the same, the hypertrophy response to training is proportionally similar, and women recover well between sets and sessions. What actually differs: Calories are lower for the same height and weight — roughly 160 kcal/day less in the Mifflin–St Jeor equation. Use the calculator with sex set correctly rather than the 2,800 default. Protein target is the same in g/lb — around 1 g per pound of bodyweight. Healthy body-fat ranges are higher. Roughly 21–31% is the normal range; essential fat is around 10–13% versus 2–5% for men. Chasing male-typical numbers is harmful and can disrupt menstrual and bone health. Upper-body strength standards are lower relative to bodyweight — largely a difference in upper-body lean mass distribution. A first pull-up typically takes longer and is a bigger achievement. Lower-body relative strength is much closer to parity, and hamstring and glute work often progresses faster. Iron intake matters more, especially if you menstruate. Low ferritin is a common and easily-missed cause of feeling flat in training. You will not "get bulky" by accident. Gaining meaningful muscle takes years of deliberate effort and eating, for everyone. Training through the menstrual cycle: current evidence does not support programming around cycle phases for most people. Some find strength dips in the days before menstruation — if so, treat it like any other bad-recovery day and reduce volume rather than restructuring the program. Worth reading: Nunes et al. (2020), Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake to support muscle mass and function in healthy adults , and the growing literature on sex differences in resistance training response — Roberts, Nuckols & Krieger (2020), Sex differences in resistance training: a systematic review and meta-analysis , Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research. find →

You still build muscle. Resistance training produces hypertrophy well into the seventies and beyond. The rate is slower, not zero, and the health return is larger. Warm up longer — 10 minutes rather than 5, and never skip the joint prep. Connective tissue adapts more slowly still. Take the rep gates even more seriously; consider adding two weeks at each rung. Protein goes up, to roughly 1.0–1.2 g/lb — older muscle is less sensitive to a given dose of protein ("anabolic resistance"), so per-meal doses matter more. Recovery between hard sessions takes longer. Three days a week is right; a fourth is usually a mistake. Deload more often — every 4–5 weeks rather than 6. Prioritize the movements you'd miss: single-leg strength, grip, and overhead range. Those are the qualities that predict independence later.

records.k: Your rungs

records.t: Rung finder Which rung are you on? Eleven questions, about two minutes. For each movement pattern, pick the hardest version you can currently do for at least 5 but no more than about 15 clean, full-range reps — that's the version you should be training. Your answers save to this browser and drive the session runner . Two rules that make this easy. If you can already do more than 15 clean reps of something, it's too easy — pick the next one up. If you can't do 5 with full range and control, it's too hard — pick the one below. Being one rung too easy costs you a week. Being one rung too hard costs you a month of half-reps and sore joints, so when you're between two, choose the easier one. I've never trained — use beginner defaults
Save and open today's session Reset all answers

Train the rung, don't skip ahead. The rep gate on each rung isn't about your muscles — those are ready long before your tendons are. It buys the connective-tissue adaptation that prevents month-four elbow and shoulder problems. Why → Move up when every set hits the top of the range with clean form and 1–2 reps left in the tank. Then reset to the bottom of the range on the new rung. That's double progression , and it's the whole progression mechanism. Expect different rungs on different patterns. Almost everyone is further along on pushing than pulling, and further along on both than on legs. That's normal, not a flaw. Redo this whenever something feels off — after a layoff, after an injury, or when an exercise stops feeling hard. It takes two minutes. Previous ← The exercise ladders Next Run today's session →
